Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Age: 67
Sex: Male
Admission Date: N/A
Discharge Date: Day 11

Summary:

A 67-year-old male with serious lung disease and heart disease came to the hospital with muscle pain and weakness in his shoulders and legs. This made it hard for him to move around. The patient was found to have muscle breakdown caused by two medicines called simvastatin and clarithromycin. Both medicines were stopped. The patient was given fluids through a vein. The patient then developed kidney problems. The kidney problems got better with fluids given through a vein. The patient worked with a physical therapist to get stronger. The patient was sent home after 11 days. His lung doctor started two new medicines for long-term use called doxycycline and ezetimibe.

Diagnosis:

Muscle breakdown caused by two medicines called simvastatin and clarithromycin

Treatment:

Fluids given through a vein, insulin with sugar water, a medicine to lower potassium levels called calcium resonium, and calcium gluconate

Concomitant Conditions:

Serious lung disease and heart disease

Follow-Up:

Follow up with his lung doctor

Documentation Source:

Clinical notes, laboratory results, and imaging reports

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Name: [Patient Name]
Age: 57
Gender: Male
Medical Record Number: [MRN]

Admission Dates:
Hospital Admission: [Date of Hospital Admission]
Discharge: [Date of Discharge]

Admitting Diagnosis:
Long-term kidney disease caused by ongoing swelling and damage to the kidney filters

Hospital Course:

This 57-year-old male patient was getting dialysis treatment at a clinic because of long-term kidney disease. Dialysis is a treatment that cleans the blood when the kidneys cannot. The kidney damage was caused by ongoing swelling in the tiny filters of the kidneys. The patient came to the hospital for an emergency kidney transplant from a donor who had died.

On the second day in the hospital, doctors checked how well the patient was eating and his body condition. The results showed he was in fairly good shape. His weight was close to what is healthy for his height. His blood test showed he had enough protein in his blood. He was eating more than 90 percent of what his body needed.

On the third day after surgery, the patient stopped fasting and started eating a special diet for kidney transplant patients.

The care team taught the patient about his special diet. They explained what foods to eat and what to watch out for. Staff checked what the patient was eating by talking with him. They changed his meals based on what foods he liked. The patient also went to a group class about eating well after a kidney transplant every Wednesday. In this class, he learned how much to eat, how to limit salt, how to eat healthy fats, why to avoid herbal products and plant supplements, and how to keep food safe and clean.

On the 16th day in the hospital, doctors checked the patient's nutrition again. The results showed he was still in fairly good shape. His weight was close to what is healthy for his height. His blood protein level was good. These results took into account how much he was eating.

Two months after leaving the hospital, the patient came back for a check-up visit. At this visit, he got advice about higher blood sugar levels after the transplant. He also got help with weight changes after leaving the hospital and high fat levels in his blood. The care team told him to drink fewer nutrition supplement drinks. They explained why keeping a healthy weight matters. They also taught him again about managing long-term health issues after a kidney transplant.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was in fairly good shape with eating and nutrition when leaving the hospital. The patient should eat a balanced diet with different healthy foods to stay healthy after going home. The patient was told to stop or cut back on nutrition supplement drinks to avoid long-term health problems. The patient should come back for regular check-up visits with the doctor.

When leaving the hospital, the patient had no health problems that needed treatment right away. The patient was stable and doing well. The patient went home with no limits on activities. The patient was told to keep taking all prescribed medicines.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Date of Discharge: March 2012
Reason for Admission: Shortness of breath, pain in the right side of the chest and upper belly area, a blood clot in the lungs, several large tumors joined together in the liver, and a liver cancer blood marker that was much higher than normal.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the Emergency Department in December 2009 with shortness of breath and pain in the right side of his chest and upper belly. Doctors found a blood clot in his lungs and several large tumors joined together in his liver. The biggest tumor measured about 6 cm x 9 cm x 9 cm and was in the right side of the liver. A tissue sample test showed the patient had liver cancer that started in the liver. The cancer was at an advanced stage and had spread to other parts of the body. He received radiation treatment to the liver, which ended in April 2010. Later scans showed the largest liver tumor had shrunk from over 14 cm to 3 cm. The cancer that had spread to his lungs was completely gone. From August 2010 to March 2012, the patient stayed healthy with normal liver test results and no signs of cancer coming back. In March 2012, doctors found a small tumor had returned in the right side of the liver. In May 2012, he had a treatment where doctors blocked blood flow to the tumor and gave cancer drugs directly to it. This treatment worked completely at that spot.

Medical Care:
The patient received radiation treatment alone for the liver tumors. For the small tumor that came back in the right liver, he had a treatment that blocked blood flow to the tumor and delivered cancer drugs directly to it.

Diagnostic Evaluation:
The patient had tests including body scans and a tissue sample test. These tests helped doctors find and track the liver tumors and the cancer that had spread to the lungs.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was stable and had no symptoms when he left the hospital in March 2012. His liver cancer blood marker dropped from 11 460 to 3.1. Scans showed no signs of cancer coming back.

Follow-Up:
The patient was told to see his doctor regularly for checkups and scans to watch for any changes.

Discharge Medications:
Not applicable.

Disposition:
The patient left the hospital in better health. His liver test results were normal. Scans showed no signs of cancer coming back.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 55 years
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the hospital with sharp chest pain on the right side that got worse with breathing. The patient also had a high fever (40ºC) and serious trouble breathing. Blood tests showed signs of infection, low oxygen levels, and high lactic acid in the blood. A chest x-ray showed an infection in the lower part of the right lung. An ultrasound of the belly showed fatty liver. The patient was diagnosed with a serious body-wide infection caused by pneumonia in the right lower lung. The patient was started on an antibiotic called piperacillin/tazobactam. On the third day of antibiotics, the patient felt pain in the upper right belly area. Doctors found that the appendix had moved under the liver, burst open, and formed a pocket of infection.

Treatment:

Doctors performed surgery using a small camera through tiny cuts in the belly. The surgery confirmed the burst appendix under the liver with a pocket of infection. The source of infection was cleaned out and controlled. A germ called Escherichia coli that does not respond to many antibiotics was found in the fluid drained during surgery. The antibiotic was changed to meropenem. The patient got better quickly after this change. The patient went home after 6 days of this targeted antibiotic treatment.

Follow-up:

The patient was told to schedule a visit with the Internal Medicine Department. The patient should keep taking the prescribed antibiotics for the full time the doctor ordered. The patient was also told to take steps to prevent future infections.

Diagnosis:

The patient had a serious body-wide infection caused by pneumonia in the right lower lung. This was followed by a burst appendix located under the liver with a pocket of infection.

Admission date: [Date of Admission]
Discharge date: [Date of Discharge]

Hospital course:
The patient, a 34-year-old woman, was admitted to the Blood Disease Department of Tor Vergata University Hospital in Rome in [Date of Admission]. She had a type of blood cancer called multiple myeloma. This cancer affects cells in the bone marrow that make antibodies. Her cancer was at an early stage. She also had a history of fever and a painful red-purple rash on her hands, forearms, and chest. This rash is called Sweet's syndrome and was caused by her cancer. A sample of her bone marrow showed that half of it was filled with cancer cells. The patient started a combination of three cancer-fighting drugs called PAD. She also took a medicine called colchicine to treat her skin rash.
The patient had a treatment to collect stem cells from her blood using a drug called cyclophosphamide. In February 2008, she received high-dose chemotherapy with a drug called melphalan. Then she had her own stem cells put back into her body. This treatment worked very well and removed most of the cancer. After that, she took medicines called bortezomib and interferon-alpha to keep the cancer away. In April 2011, her cancer came back. The skin rash also returned at the same time. Both were treated with colchicine and two other medicines called Lenalidomide and Dexamethasone. Each time the cancer came back after that, the skin rash also came back. The rash went away each time with colchicine and the right cancer treatment.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Multiple myeloma, a blood cancer
2. Sweet's syndrome, a skin condition caused by the cancer

Disposition:
The patient was sent to [Disposition] in stable condition. She was told to schedule a follow-up visit with the Blood Disease Department of Tor Vergata University Hospital in Rome.

items.clean_ref:
Patient Information:
Name: [Patient Name]
DOB: [Patient Date of Birth]
Gender: [Patient Gender]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital at nineteen months old. The patient had repeated lung infections and a heart problem called patent ductus arteriosus. This means a blood vessel near the heart did not close after birth like it should. The patient had a procedure to close this blood vessel using a small device. During the procedure, the doctors found that a large vein in the belly was not formed the normal way. The blood was flowing through a different path using other veins. The doctors placed a thin tube through a vein in the neck to complete the procedure.

Post-Procedure:
After the procedure, pictures of the heart and blood vessels showed the device was in the right place. There was no blood leaking around it. More heart pictures were taken later. These showed that blood was flowing normally to the heart. A special test of the veins was done to check how the blood was moving. It showed blood flowing through the belly veins and other veins in a normal way.

Diagnosis:
Patent ductus arteriosus, which is a blood vessel near the heart that did not close after birth.

Treatment:
The patient had a procedure to close the open blood vessel. The doctors used a small device called a Heartr duct occluder. They placed a thin tube through a vein in the neck because the usual path through other veins was twisted and hard to use.

Prognosis:
The pictures taken after the procedure showed the device stayed in place. No blood was leaking around it. Later heart pictures showed blood was flowing normally to the heart.

Recommendations:
The patient should see their childrens doctor for more check-ups. The doctor will watch how the patient is doing and help manage the condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 9 years
Gender: Female
Diagnoses: Early puberty, a non-cancerous liver growth called focal nodular hyperplasia

Hospital Course:
The patient came to Dongguan Children's Hospital 6 months ago because her breasts started developing. Doctors ran blood tests and took pictures of the inside of her body. They found she had early puberty and a non-cancerous growth on her liver. The patient received a shot in the muscle once a month of a medicine called triptorelin to slow down early puberty. The patient had a procedure to destroy the liver growth using heat from a small needle. Doctors also took a tiny sample of the growth to study it. They put the patient to sleep with a breathing tube during the procedure. They added fluid to her belly area to help see the growth better on the screen. The procedure went well. The patient went home on the sixth day after the procedure. She was given germ-fighting medicine called cefixime granules. She also received a liver-protecting medicine called compound glycyrrhizin capsules. One month later, a detailed body scan showed the growth was fully destroyed. The scan also showed her gallbladder was not harmed. Three months after that, another imaging test showed the treated area looked the same. There was no blood flowing into the treated spot.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient should keep taking her medicines as directed. The patient should see her doctors for check-ups as planned. The patient may need regular visits and imaging tests to watch the treated area.

Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Early puberty
2. A non-cancerous liver growth called focal nodular hyperplasia

Discharge Condition:
The patient was in stable condition when she left the hospital.

Hospital Course:
The patient was a 23-year-old female admitted to our facility. She had trouble breathing, a dry cough, chills, felt unwell, and was sweating a lot. She recently had COVID-19 and had poorly controlled diabetes. She was taking dulaglutide and empagliflozin for her diabetes. During the exam, the patient had a fast heartbeat and was breathing quickly. Blood tests showed serious problems with the body's acid levels. The acid-buffering level was very low at 11, and the acid gap was high at 23. Urine tests showed sugar, protein, and acids called ketones. The patient was admitted to the hospital to treat the high acid levels in her blood. She did not need treatment for COVID-19. On day 2, the acid-buffering level dropped from 11 to 6, and the acid gap rose to 24. The patient was given insulin and a drip to lower acid levels. On day 3, the acid gap dropped to 16. The insulin drip was stopped, and the patient switched to insulin shots. The patient got better with treatment, and her symptoms improved. Later blood tests kept showing good progress, and acid levels returned to normal. A review of her records showed the patient should have been on insulin. She had not been keeping her appointments with her diabetes doctor.

Discharge Diagnosis:
A dangerous buildup of acids in the blood with normal blood sugar levels, caused by the diabetes medicine Jardiance and a recent COVID-19 infection

Discharge Instructions:
1. Stop taking Jardiance
2. Keep taking insulin shots as directed
3. See a diabetes doctor for a follow-up visit

Follow-Up:
The patient should see a diabetes doctor to check blood sugar levels and manage her diabetes.

items.clean_ref:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient: 79-year-old male

Medications: None prescribed

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with pain in the right side of the back that had lasted for 1 year. During the exam, the patient's heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature were normal. The belly was soft and not painful when pressed. There was no swelling of organs or lumps that could be felt.

Blood tests and urine hormone tests came back normal. The urine test showed signs of possible infection. However, the lab test to grow bacteria found no germs after 24 hours.

A CT scan with dye showed a large growth behind the belly area near the right adrenal gland. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. The growth had brighter edges, dead tissue in the center, and small calcium spots. The dye washed out of the growth over time. An MRI scan with dye also showed a large uneven growth with dead tissue in the center above the right kidney. The edges of the growth showed up brighter on the scan.

Surgery was done to remove the right adrenal gland. The patient did well after surgery with no problems. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed the growth was a cavernous hemangioma. This is a non-cancerous tumor made of tangled blood vessels.

Follow-up:

The patient has healed well after surgery. The patient should schedule regular visits with the regular doctor. No other tests are needed. No medications have been prescribed at discharge.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 78-year-old female, was sent to the eye department at University Hospital Bonn for urgent care. She had blurry vision, blind spots, and saw flashing lights. She also had a dry cough for four months that did not get better with treatment or antibiotics.

Over the past five weeks, the patient had growing pain on both sides of her jaw and sharp pain in her tongue. This made it hard for her to swallow. She also lost weight, felt more tired, had mild fevers, and had a tender scalp.

Visits to a dentist, an orthodontist, and an ear, nose, and throat doctor did not find any problems. A brain and nerve exam was normal. A chest X-ray showed no issues.

Blood tests showed signs of swelling in the body. An eye exam showed swelling of the nerve at the back of the left eye. There were also white patches near blood vessels in the left eye. Special eye scans and dye tests confirmed the nerve in the left eye was damaged from poor blood flow.

An ultrasound of the blood vessels in the head and neck showed swelling of the vessel walls in many areas. This swelling was seen in the blood vessels near the temples on both sides of the head. It was also in the forehead and side branches of those vessels. The right cheek artery and right armpit artery were also affected. Blood vessels in the neck and under the tongue showed the same signs of swelling.

The patient was diagnosed with giant cell arteritis based on her symptoms, exam, blood tests, and ultrasound. This is a condition where blood vessel walls become swollen and inflamed. Treatment was started right away. The patient first received 500 mg of a strong anti-swelling medicine called methylprednisolone through an IV each day. Then she took 60 mg of prednisolone by mouth each day. This dose was slowly lowered over 26 weeks. She also started getting 162 mg of tocilizumab by injection under the skin once a week. This was given because many blood vessels were affected.

With treatment, the patient's symptoms and blood test results got better quickly. Her jaw and tongue pain went away within days. She left the hospital five days later in stable condition. Three months later, she came back for a check-up. She was taking 9 mg of prednisolone each day and 162 mg of tocilizumab by injection each week. She had no symptoms. The ultrasound showed the blood vessel walls were much less swollen.

Six months after leaving the hospital, the patient came back for another check-up. Her vision had improved. An eye exam showed less swelling of the nerve in the left eye, but the nerve looked pale with narrow blood vessels. She was taking 12.5 mg of prednisolone each day and 162 mg of tocilizumab by injection each week. She had no symptoms. The ultrasound showed the blood vessel walls were even less swollen than before.

The patient has been told to keep following her treatment plan. She should schedule regular check-ups to watch her condition.

Diagnoses:

The patient left the hospital after finishing 21 days of ceftriaxone, 7 days of methylprednisolone, 7 days of doxycycline, and 5 days of human immunoglobulin. This treatment raised his CD4 count and lowered the virus to levels too small to measure.

Patient: 36-year-old prisoner

Diagnosis: Fungal infection causing a pocket of pus in the lung

Hospital Course:
The patient came to our hospital with fever, weakness, cough, and coughing up blood. These symptoms did not get better with antibiotics. The patient received fluconazole 400 mg through a vein first, then as pills until fully recovered. The patient was then sent home. The patient was given an appointment to follow up with our liver care team and start hepatitis C treatment. After three months of taking sofosbuvir 400 mg and velpatasvir 100 mg once a day, the hepatitis C virus was no longer found in the blood. This result is still holding.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was given an appointment to follow up with our liver care team. This is to keep managing the liver disease caused by hepatitis C. The patient was also told to keep healthy habits and to stop using drugs.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with fever, dry cough, trouble breathing, and wheezing sounds. Doctors first thought the patient had a lung infection caught outside the hospital. The patient received antibiotics through a vein, steroid pills, and breathing treatments through a mist machine. The treatment did not work well, and the patient's breathing got worse. The patient came back to the hospital. Tests showed too many white blood cells called eosinophils in the blood. A tissue sample showed the lungs were swollen due to these cells. After death, an exam of the body found too many eosinophil cells in all organs. Special lab tests showed signs of T-cell cancer. This confirmed the patient had a fast-spreading type of blood cancer.

Deceased. The patient died while in the hospital.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
This 54-year-old man was healthy before this illness. He was admitted for bleeding on the surface of his brain. He also had weakness and reduced feeling on the left side of his body. For two weeks before coming to the hospital, he had headaches and neck pain that kept getting worse. He also felt dizzy. The headache was a pressing pain felt all over his head. The pain changed a lot depending on his body position. The patient developed numbness in his left arm and leg and then fell down. He was first taken to another hospital. Doctors there found a bruised cut on the left side of his head near his temple. The patient was then moved to this hospital for more tests and treatment.

Diagnostic Testing:
A CT scan of the head showed bleeding on the brain surface in the right front and side areas. It also showed a small blood clot about 8 mm wide in the right side of the brain. Doctors thought this was likely caused by an abnormal blood vessel. A CT scan of the blood vessels in the head showed that a vessel in the front of the brain was smaller than normal. A special test using dye to look at blood vessels found no bulging vessels or tangled blood vessels. However, it did show a blockage in a vein on the right side of the brain surface. Dye was slow to drain from a large vein on the left side of the brain. This suggested mildly high pressure inside the skull. An MRI scan of the brain showed the covering of the brain lighting up after dye was given. This suggested low spinal fluid pressure. The MRI also showed a small fresh blood clot on the right side of the brain.

Treatment:
The patient was given nimodipine, a medicine to prevent blood vessel spasms. He also received heparin shots under the skin to prevent blood clots. Later he was switched to blood thinner pills taken by mouth. The weakness and numbness went away. However, his headaches continued. Doctors then did a blood patch, where blood is injected near the spine. This treatment made all his symptoms go away completely.

Follow-up:
The patient left the hospital in good health. He was given instructions for ongoing care. He should keep all follow-up appointments with his doctor. He should also follow a healthy lifestyle. This will help prevent future problems or symptoms from coming back.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]

Patient Name: [name]
Medical Record Number: [number]

Diagnosis: A non-cancerous tumor on the pituitary gland that makes too much thyroid-stimulating hormone, causing an overactive thyroid

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 55-year-old man, came to the hospital after being moved from another hospital. He was found to have an irregular heartbeat by chance. After a procedure to fix his irregular heartbeat, doctors found his thyroid hormone levels were too high. Blood tests showed antibodies attacking his thyroid. His thyroid gland was larger than normal and had a lump in the left side. A test using a thin needle showed the lump was not cancer. A brain scan showed a tumor on the pituitary gland. The tumor was about 2.3 by 1.7 by 2.2 centimeters. It was growing into nearby areas at the base of the brain. Based on these results, doctors found the patient had a pituitary tumor that was making his thyroid overactive.

One week after finding the tumor, the patient had surgery through the nose to remove it. Tests on the removed tumor showed it made thyroid-stimulating hormone and another hormone called prolactin. The tumor was not cancer. After surgery, the patient's thyroid hormone levels went back to normal.

One year after surgery, the patient's thyroid hormone levels went up again. No tumor was found on the brain scan. Blood tests showed antibodies attacking the thyroid were still present. The patient was given a medicine called thyrozol at 10 milligrams per day. This medicine kept thyroid levels normal for three years.

During the hospital stay, there were no major problems. The patient was sent home with instructions to keep taking thyrozol 10 milligrams per day. The patient was told to see a hormone specialist for more care.

Disposition:

The patient went home in stable condition. The patient was told to see a hormone specialist for follow-up care. The patient was given thyrozol 10 milligrams per day. The patient was told to keep taking this medicine as directed. The patient was told to come back to the hospital if there were any concerns or changes in how they feel.

The parents are not related by blood. No one else in the family has the same condition.

On the outside of the body, the doctor found crusty sores on the backs of the hands and elbows. There were also lighter, darker, or pale scars on the back, arms, elbows, and backs of the hands. Small bumps that look like beads were found on the eyelids of both eyes.

The patient was started on Acitretin 10 mg per day. This is a medicine that helps with skin problems.
The patient was sent to the ear, nose, and throat doctors and skin doctors. They started speech therapy. Skin moisturizers were also given.

Hospital Course:
The sores happened less often and left fewer scars. The patient was sent to other doctors for more care.

The patient, a 55-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital after she suddenly had a severe headache, fainted, felt weakness on the left side of her body, and had trouble speaking. A brain scan showed swelling around it. A test that looks at blood vessels in the brain showed inflamed blood vessels on the right side of the brain. The test also showed a small bulge in a blood vessel and a widened area in another blood vessel on the left side of the brain. A small sample of brain tissue was taken and tested. It showed signs of inflammation with certain white blood cells gathering around blood vessels in the brain covering.

Treatment:

The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close watching and treatment. She was given high doses of a strong anti-inflammatory medicine called methylprednisolone through her vein for three days. She was also given a medicine called cyclophosphamide through her vein once a month for six doses. This medicine helps calm down the immune system. She left the hospital with a prescription for prednisolone, a steroid medicine, at a dose based on her weight. She was also given phenytoin, a medicine to prevent seizures, at 300 mg per day.

Follow-up:

The patient is now being checked every month. She is taking cyclophosphamide and prednisolone by mouth. Her doses are being slowly lowered over time.

The patient came to the hospital for more tests related to Parkinson disease at age 63. He has a family history of Parkinson disease and also has depression. The patient's treatment plan stayed the same during this hospital stay. A speech therapist helped him continue eating regular food safely to prevent food or liquid from going into the lungs.

Follow-up:
The patient will see his doctor to check on how his Parkinson disease is doing over time.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 12-year-old Japanese girl (III-1 in Fig. b)

Medical History: The patient has had fevers that keep coming back, belly pain, loose stools, ankle joint pain, mouth sores, sore throat, and swollen tonsils since she was 2 months old. She also had sores around her bottom, blood in her stool, and weight loss at ages 4 and 5. At 9 years old, doctors found swelling in her left ankle joint. She was given naproxen and methotrexate, but these were stopped because of belly pain. She was then treated with colchicine and mesalazine for belly pain. Later, doctors found many sores throughout her digestive tract. At 11 years old, she was found to have eye swelling in both eyes without lumpy tissue buildup. She was also diagnosed with Behcet's disease, a condition that causes ongoing inflammation in different parts of the body.

Hospital Course: The patient was treated with colchicine, cimetidine, and steroid eye drops. Her belly pain has gotten better. Her fevers do not happen as often.

Assessment and Plan: The patient should keep taking colchicine, cimetidine, and steroid eye drops. Follow-up visits will be set up as needed. More check-ups and tests will be talked about when necessary.

Discharge Diagnosis: Behcet's disease affecting the digestive system and eye swelling in the front part of both eyes without lumpy tissue buildup.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 67 years
Sex: Female

Chief Complaint:
Medium-grade colon cancer in the right side of the colon.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with medium-grade cancer in the right side of the colon. Surgery was done to remove the right part of the colon. Lab tests confirmed stage III cancer that had spread to nearby lymph nodes. The patient started cancer-killing drug treatment but had to stop after four of eight rounds. This was because of serious nerve damage in the hands and feet. After finishing treatment, the patient had regular check-ups to watch for cancer return. In November 2012, the cancer came back near a muscle in the lower back area. It was removed by surgery in December. Special lab tests showed a problem with how the body fixes damaged genes. The patient received radiation treatment along with a cancer pill called capecitabine. But the patient's white blood cell count dropped too low. The dose of capecitabine had to be lowered. In October 2013, the cancer came back in a bone in the lower spine. The patient received focused radiation treatment in 10 sessions. In June 2014, the cancer returned in the same spot. The patient had surgery to remove the growth to help with symptoms.

Enter Personalized OncoGenomics (POG) initiative:
The patient agreed to have the tumor from the spine tested for gene changes. This was done by the POG program at the BC Cancer Agency. The gene tests showed that certain genes called FOS and JUN were too active. These genes control cell growth. Lab tests confirmed high levels of a protein called c-JUN. Doctors suggested trying a blood pressure drug called irbesartan. This drug might help by blocking a body system that could be helping the cancer grow.

Treatment:
The patient had a full body scan before starting treatment. The patient began taking irbesartan at 150 mg once a day in December 2014. After 5 weeks of treatment, another full body scan was done. The scan showed the cancer was almost completely gone. A blood test that measures cancer activity dropped from 18 to 3.1.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Medium-grade colon cancer in the right side of the colon.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been discharged, and her condition is stable. Follow-up visits have been scheduled. Instructions for medicine and diet have been given.

Medications:
Irbesartan 150 mg once a day.

Follow-up:
Follow-up appointments have been scheduled. The patient has been told to eat healthy foods and live a healthy lifestyle. The patient should keep taking medicine as directed.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient first came to the hospital for hip pain. After more tests, doctors found the patient has lung cancer. The cancer had spread to the liver and a bone in the hip area. The cancer cells are fast-growing and hard to identify. During the hospital stay, the patient became confused at times. The patient also saw things that were not there and became restless. More tests showed the patient had a fungal infection in the brain and spinal fluid. This infection is called Cryptococcal meningitis. Doctors treated this infection with two anti-fungal medicines called Flucytosine and amphotericin. The patient's thinking got better after four days on these medicines. After twelve days, the patient's mind was back to normal. The patient also had ten radiation treatments to help with pain and slow the cancer. These treatments went well with no problems. The patient went home with a lower dose of an anti-fungal medicine called fluconazole. This medicine will help keep the fungal infection from coming back.

Summary of Care:

The hospital stay had some problems. The Flucytosine medicine caused a very low white blood cell count. This makes it harder to fight infections. The medicine also caused problems with the body's minerals and salts. The patient also had low sodium levels in the blood. This happened because of a hormone problem linked to the lung cancer. This condition is called SIADH. It makes the body hold on to too much water.

Outpatient Follow-up:

The patient needs to see the cancer care team for more treatment of the lung cancer. The patient must keep taking fluconazole for a long time. This will help prevent the fungal brain infection from coming back.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Lung cancer that has spread to the liver and a bone in the hip area. The cancer cells are fast-growing and hard to identify.
2. Fungal infection in the brain and spinal fluid called Cryptococcal meningitis.

Discharge Condition:

The patient is leaving the hospital in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: __________
Age: 23 years
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: __________
Date of Discharge: __________

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the Outpatients Department of the Ophthalmiatreio Eye Hospital of Athens. The patient had worsening vision in the right eye and saw flashing lights in both eyes. The patient had a full eye exam. The doctors asked about the patient's eye and general health history. They checked how well the patient could see with glasses. They looked at the front and back parts of both eyes using a special microscope. The patient had several tests done. These included tests to check side vision and tests using special dyes to look at blood vessels in the eyes. The patient also had scans to take detailed pictures of the back of the eyes. The patient had tests to measure how well the eyes respond to light and patterns. These tests followed standards set by an international group of eye experts. Based on the results, the doctors found that the patient had AZOOR.

Two months after the first visit, the doctors checked the patient again. Vision in the right eye had gotten worse, dropping to 20/63. Vision in the left eye stayed normal at 20/20. The side vision test was done again. It showed more vision loss in the right eye. The left eye now also showed some problems. The doctors followed the patient for 8 more months. During this time, the symptoms and exam findings stayed the same in both eyes. The patient also had scans of the head and belly. These scans did not show any problems.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy, also called AZOOR. This is a rare condition that affects the outer layer of the back of the eye.

Plan:
The patient was sent home. The patient was told to come back for regular checkups and ongoing care.

Prognosis:
The symptoms and exam findings stayed stable in both eyes after 8 months of checkups.

The patient will keep coming back to the clinic for checkups. Blood tests will be done from time to time to make sure her thyroid hormone levels stay normal.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Confidential
Medical Record Number: Confidential
Date of Admission: Confidential
Date of Discharge: Confidential

Hospital Course:
The patient is an 82-year-old female. She came to the hospital as an emergency with a very swollen belly and pain in the lower belly. For six weeks before this, she had been feeling unwell, not wanting to eat, and feeling dizzy. She also had a long history of trouble passing stool. Her past health problems included high blood pressure and blood sugar levels that were higher than normal. She had a past surgery to deliver a baby.

During the exam, the patient had a very swollen belly that did not hurt when touched. There was a soft mass in the lower left side of her belly. Blood tests showed her kidneys had suddenly stopped working well. The tests also showed she had low iron in her blood. A scan showed her large bowel was very stretched and full of stool. This was blocking both tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. The doctors decided to do surgery. During surgery, they found the lower part of her large bowel was very stretched. They also found thick scar tissue around the end of the bowel. The doctors removed part of the bowel and created an opening in the belly for waste to leave the body. After surgery, her kidneys started working normally again. She recovered well without any problems.

The doctors looked at the removed bowel tissue under a microscope. They found that the muscle layer running along the length of the bowel was damaged and missing in many areas. The nerve networks in the bowel wall were damaged where the muscle was missing. There were unusual clumps of a starchy substance in the muscle layers. The muscle layer running along the bowel was almost completely damaged. This pointed to a disease of the muscle itself. The muscle loss happened in areas where the outer lining and inner lining were still healthy. This meant the muscle disease was the main problem and not caused by something else. Muscle cells in both muscle layers were replaced by stretchy tissue and scar tissue. There was also extra stretchy tissue in other layers. Normal tissue had changed into smooth muscle tissue in many areas.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was found to have sudden kidney failure and a very stretched lower large bowel with thick scar tissue around the end of the bowel. Looking at the removed tissue showed a muscle disease with stretchy tissue and scar tissue.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient should eat healthy foods and exercise regularly. She should go to all follow-up visits with her healthcare provider. She should also take steps to prevent trouble passing stool. This includes eating more fiber and drinking plenty of water.

Discharge Medications:
None.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should not do hard physical work. She should rest well for at least two weeks after the surgery. She should go to all follow-up visits with her healthcare provider. These visits will check how her kidneys and bowel are working. They will also make sure she is healing well after surgery. If there are any bad effects or problems, the patient should contact her healthcare provider right away.

Discharge Date: [date]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital because of trouble walking that got worse over time. The patient also had many falls. The patient showed slow thinking and had trouble paying attention. The patient also could not control their bladder. A medicine called L-dopa did not help. During the exam, doctors found slow and stiff movement in the arms and legs. The patient had sudden muscle twitches in the arms. The patient had trouble feeling things through touch and did not notice things on one side of the body. The patient also showed certain reflex actions, especially grabbing things without meaning to. Memory and thinking tests showed medium-stage memory loss. The patient had trouble with planning, remembering, and drawing shapes. The patient also had trouble using their hands to do tasks on purpose. Based on all these findings, doctors diagnosed the patient with corticobasal syndrome. This is a brain condition that affects movement and thinking.

Diagnostic Findings:
Brain scans showed signs of fluid buildup in the brain. This is called normal pressure hydrocephalus. The scans also showed some damage to small blood vessels in the brain. Doctors did a spinal tap test by removing some fluid from the spine. After this test, the patient's thinking got better, but walking did not improve. Tests on the spinal fluid showed changes that match Alzheimer's disease.

Overall Assessment and Plan:
The patient has corticobasal syndrome. The patient also has signs of fluid buildup in the brain and small blood vessel damage. While in the hospital, the patient got treatment to help with symptoms. The patient should see their regular doctor and a brain specialist after leaving the hospital. The patient needs more tests, including brain scans. The patient also needs follow-up tests on spinal fluid.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification: Baby S P, 6-year-old girl

Hospital Course:
Baby S P came to the hospital because her breasts were growing on both sides, she was having monthly bleeding from her private area, and hair was growing in her private area. She had also grown taller recently. She did not have neck swelling, dark skin patches, bone pain or breaks, or growth of her private parts. Her birth and early baby period were normal.

During the physical exam, her heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature were normal. She did not have thyroid swelling, light brown skin spots, or bone problems. Her breast and pubic hair development were at stage 3. She had no underarm hair or unclear private parts. Her heart, chest, brain, and belly exams were all normal.

Blood tests showed normal blood cell counts, liver function, kidney function, and thyroid function. However, her hormone tests showed low levels of LH and FSH, which are hormones that control growth and development. Her testosterone and DHEAS levels were high. A scan of her lower belly showed her left ovary was large, measuring 5.4 cm. It was mostly solid with small fluid sacs around the edges. Her uterus looked like it was developing.

The patient had surgery using small cuts and a camera to remove a growth from her right ovary and tube. Lab tests on the growth showed it was a type of tumor made of mixed cell types. After surgery, she had bleeding from her private area for 72 hours. A hormone test done 6 days after surgery showed her estradiol levels had gone down.

At her 6-month checkup, she had no bleeding from her private area.

Diagnosis: A tumor made of mixed cell types found in the ovary area

Follow-up: At the 6-month checkup, there was no bleeding from the private area.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:

This 9-year-old boy came to the hospital because he was having trouble seeing clearly. Eye tests showed he was slightly farsighted. Even with glasses, he could only see about one-third as well as normal in both eyes. When doctors looked at the back of his eyes, they saw a wheel-shaped pattern in the center and a golden-yellow color in the lower outer areas. A test that measures how the eye responds to light showed the signals were much weaker than normal. Tests of his side vision showed blind spots near the center in both eyes. His ability to see colors was normal. A special scan confirmed that the layers in the center of his eye were splitting apart. During the visit, the patient's mother's brother was also found to have the same eye condition that runs in families.

Diagnostic Testing:

After the family agreed, doctors did complete eye exams and gene tests on all available family members of the affected boy. They took blood samples and studied the genetic material from the blood. They looked at a specific gene called XLRS1 that is linked to this eye condition. They found a change in the gene where two building blocks were swapped, causing the wrong protein to be made. This same gene change was found in his sister, mother, and mother's brother.

Impression:

The summary shows that the patient has an inherited eye condition that affects the back of the eye. This condition is passed down through families and mainly affects boys. The gene tests found a change in the XLRS1 gene. This same change was found in other family members. The family should meet with a genetic counselor to talk about what these results mean and how this condition might affect other family members.

Plan:

The doctors talked with the family about the gene test results and what problems this eye condition can cause. The patient was sent home with instructions to see an eye doctor for more care after talking with the physician. The treatment plan will depend on how serious the condition is and how it changes over time. The plan will also depend on the patient's own needs. Regular eye checkups are needed to watch for any changes or new problems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: XXXX, Age: 5 years

Admission Date: DD/MM/YYYY
Discharge Date: DD/MM/YYYY

Main Problem: Thick rubbery mucus blocking the airways, causing breathing failure.

What Happened Before Coming to the Hospital: The patient is a 5-year-old boy. He came to the hospital because thick rubbery mucus was blocking his airways. This made it hard for him to breathe. At age 2, the patient had a major heart surgery called a Fontan procedure. Since that surgery, the patient has often had breathing problems from this thick rubbery mucus.

Past Health Problems: Right after birth, the patient was found to have several heart problems. The heart had holes and parts that did not form correctly. Some blood vessels were also too narrow or blocked. The patient had four heart surgeries to fix these problems. These surgeries happened at 6 days old, 5 months old, 1 year old, and 2 years 3 months old.

Family Health History: No important family health problems were noted.

What Happened During the Hospital Stay: The patient was scheduled for a procedure to block abnormal fluid channels in the lungs. A thin tube would be placed through the skin to do this. On the morning of the procedure, the patient coughed up a mucus plug. The patient had no fever and was active. When doctors looked at the throat, they saw a lot of mucus in the upper airway. The tissue around the voice box was also swollen. After placing a breathing tube, thick pale yellow mucus came out. Doctors had to suction it out many times. The doctors thought the airway was blocked by mucus plugs. The procedure was delayed. Doctors tried to remove the mucus using a thin camera tube placed into the airways. There was too much mucus to see clearly. The patient coughed, and a thick rubbery mucus plug shaped like the airways came out through the breathing tube. The patient was moved to another hospital. The airway became blocked again. A machine was used to help pump blood and add oxygen outside the body for a short time. Six days later, the patient was taken off the breathing machine. The patient was sent home with no signs of brain damage.

Physical Exam Findings: When the patient arrived, the neck veins were swollen. A soft heart sound was heard on the left side of the chest. Breathing sounds were normal. A chest X-ray showed an enlarged heart and fluid buildup in the lungs. A heart rhythm test showed the electrical signals in the heart were slightly off. It also showed the right side of the heart was thicker than normal. A heart ultrasound showed a small opening between heart chambers. There was a tiny leak in one of the heart valves. The large vein bringing blood back to the heart was not blocked.

Diagnosis: Thick rubbery mucus blocking the airways, causing breathing failure.

Treatment: A low-fat diet and breathing exercises did not help. Medicines to open the airways, loosen mucus, and improve blood flow in the lungs also did not help. The planned procedure to block abnormal fluid channels was delayed. This was because mucus plugs were blocking the airway. Doctors tried to remove the mucus with a thin camera tube but could not. The patient coughed up a thick rubbery mucus plug shaped like the airways. Doctors gave medicine through the breathing tube to break up clots. They also gave medicine to open the airways. Another medicine was given through an IV to reduce swelling.

Condition at Discharge: Stable and better.

Instructions for Home: The patient should keep taking all prescribed medicines. The patient should see the healthcare provider for regular checkups. The family should keep the home clean and free of dust and allergens. This helps reduce things in the air that can irritate the lungs. The patient and family should learn how to use the medicines correctly. They should also have a plan for emergencies and know when to come back for appointments. The patient should see a childrens doctor, a lung specialist, and a heart doctor for ongoing care.

The patient is a 43-year-old woman who never smoked. The patient was admitted after having trouble breathing during activity for six months. The patient had several tests done to find the cause. These tests included a chest X-ray and CT scan of the chest. The patient also had a scope passed into the lungs to collect samples. Brain scans and full body scans were also done. These tests showed advanced small cell lung cancer that had spread. The patient started the first round of cancer-fighting drugs called cisplatin and etoposide. The tumor got much smaller with this treatment. After six rounds, the cancer started growing again. The patient then started a second set of drugs called carboplatin and irinotecan. After two rounds, the patient got a lung infection caused by a blockage. The treatment plan had to change. The cancer was no longer responding to standard treatments. The patient started a third set of drugs called CAV. This included three medicines: Adriamycin, vincristine, and cyclophosphamide. The patient received 11 rounds of this treatment. After the 11th round, the cancer started growing again. This treatment could not continue. The patient then started a fourth set of drugs called ICE. This included ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide. The patient had to stop because of bad side effects. A new plan using ICE without etoposide was started as the fourth treatment. The cancer partly shrank with this treatment. The patient's pain slowly went away during this time. The patient chose to stop further treatment. Eight months after finishing five rounds of carboplatin and ifosfamide, the patient came to the emergency room. The patient had trouble breathing and rib pain. A chest CT scan showed the tumor had grown larger. Comfort care was started with a sixth round of carboplatin and ifosfamide. The patient's symptoms got better. Sadly, the patient died from a lung infection caused by food or liquid going into the lungs. This happened 11 days later. The patient lived for about 27 months after starting cancer treatment.

The patient started having seizures one day after he was born. These seizures caused his arms and legs to stiffen and stretch out. The seizures stopped after the dose was raised to 12.5 milligrams for each kilogram of body weight per day. The brain wave test got better and no longer showed the problem pattern.

MEDICATIONS:
The patient takes phenytoin. This medicine worked well to stop his seizures.

The patient will keep seeing his doctors for regular checkups.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 45-year-old man. He came to the hospital with fever, chills, sweating, headache, muscle pain that came and went, and a weight loss of 22 pounds. He worked with farm animals in the past. He had no history of heart problems. During the exam, the doctor heard an abnormal heart sound. Blood tests showed signs of infection and some liver problems. The chest X-ray and heart rhythm test looked normal. A scan of the belly area showed an enlarged spleen with a pocket of infection in part of it. A heart ultrasound showed small growths on two parts of a heart valve. The patient was found to have brucellosis, an infection caught from animals. This was proven by testing the blood. The patient received three antibiotics called gentamycin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. He got better after four days of treatment. He left the hospital after 16 days. He was told to come back for follow-up visits.

Follow-Up:
The patient was checked regularly and given more antibiotics. These were trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, rifampicin, and doxycycline. After one month, blood tests showed much less infection. After two months, a detailed heart ultrasound showed one growth on the heart valve was gone. The other growth stayed the same size. After seven months, another heart ultrasound showed all the growths were completely gone. The patient took antibiotics for 12 months total. He had no side effects from the medicine. One year after finishing the medicine, the patient had more tests done. A belly scan showed the spleen was back to normal size. The pocket of infection had changed but no new pockets formed. Blood tests showed the infection markers were much lower. No bacteria were found in the blood. The patient has continued to be checked. He shows no signs of the infection coming back.

Diagnosis:
The patient was found to have brucellosis. This was proven by blood tests.

Treatment:
The patient received three antibiotics called gentamycin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. After leaving the hospital, the patient received trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, rifampicin, and doxycycline. The patient took antibiotics for 12 months total. Follow-up tests showed he was getting better.

Prognosis:
The patient has fully recovered from brucellosis. The enlarged spleen is back to normal. The infection has not come back. Follow-up tests continue to show good results.

Diagnosis: Mild Learning Disability with a Mental Health Condition Causing False Beliefs and Hearing Things That Are Not Real

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 28-year-old male. He came to the hospital because he had been acting irritable and talking to himself for 12 years. He also heard songs that were not real. During the mental health exam, the patient believed that random events had special meaning about him. He also heard voices talking to him that were not real. Testing showed his thinking and learning skills are below average. Based on these findings, the doctors found he has a mild learning disability and a mental health condition. The patient was given olanzapine 10 mg pills and sodium valproate 1000 mg pills. These medicines worked well for him.

Patient Progress:
While in the hospital, the patient got much better. His irritable behavior and hearing things that are not real improved a lot. He also started sleeping and eating better. The doctor decided the patient was stable enough to go home. The patient was told to keep taking his medicines. He was also told to go to his follow-up mental health visits. He should follow the treatment plan given to him.

The patient was given these instructions before leaving the hospital:
Keep taking the medicines as written on the prescription.
Go to all scheduled mental health visits so the doctor can check on symptoms and progress.
Tell the doctor if any new symptoms or side effects happen.
Follow the treatment plan including eating well, exercising, and making healthy lifestyle changes.
If there is an emergency, call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital for help.

Follow-up Care:
The patient should see his mental health doctor at the scheduled times. The patient and his family were told why regular mental health visits are important. These visits help make sure the treatment is working. They also help address any worries or problems with the patient's condition.

They also learned why regular visits with the doctor are needed.

Discharge Date:

Primary Diagnosis: Severe lung infection and breathing failure

Hospital Course:
A 13-year-old female was admitted to the hospital for a severe lung infection and breathing failure. The patient has a history of lung infections, an underactive thyroid, and stomach lining swelling. Lab tests at admission showed higher than normal white blood cells, blood clotting cells, and signs of swelling in the body. During the hospital stay, the patient was put on a breathing machine and given strong germ-fighting medicines through a vein for a bacterial infection. The patient also received physical therapy to help clear the lungs. Medicines to reduce swelling were given by mouth and through a breathing device for a short time.

Secondary Diagnosis:
Damaged and widened airways in several areas of the lungs with swelling of the small airways
Protein in the urine

Tests and Procedures:
Detailed X-ray scan of the chest
Test to check for cystic fibrosis using sweat
Tissue sample taken from the inside of the nose
Tissue sample taken from the kidney using imaging to guide the needle

Lab Test Results:
Tests of the body's defense system were normal, except for a small increase in allergy-related proteins
Tests for a specific germ that causes lung infections were negative
A protein that shows swelling in the body was high

Consultations:
Tests of the body's defense system

Follow-Up:
Repeat chest X-rays and detailed scans showed no major changes. Kidney function tests and protein in the urine were slightly high. The protein that shows swelling in the body went down a little at the most recent visit.

Medications:
None specified in the case report.

Discharge Disposition:
The patient was sent home and should follow up with their regular doctor for ongoing care. No future hospital stays are expected for this condition.

Patient Name: [Name]
Age: 37
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: [Admission Date]
Date of Discharge: [Discharge Date]
Admitting Physician: [Physician Name]
Primary Diagnosis: Hives

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the allergy clinic with a problem of hives that kept coming back all over her body. She also had a rash and swelling of her face. These problems got worse when she ate very spicy foods, heavily seasoned foods, or Chinese foods. In the past, she was treated for allergies that caused a stuffy or runny nose. She also had bad hives and a rash all over her body after taking pain medicines like ibuprofen. Blood tests showed she had higher than normal levels of certain allergy-related cells and proteins. A skin test showed small reactions to silkworm pupa, herring, cabbage, celery, and walnut. However, the patient had never gotten hives from eating any of these foods before.

The patient had a special blood test to check how her allergy cells react to different things. The test showed that her allergy cells reacted to MSG, a flavor enhancer often used in food. Her allergy cells did not react to any other food additives that were tested. Tests for thyroid hormone levels came back normal.

The patient was told she has hives. She was told to stay away from foods that seem to cause her symptoms. No medicines were given.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was given information on how to take care of her symptoms at home. She was told to avoid foods that seem to cause her hives. She was also told to come back to the clinic if her symptoms do not go away or get worse.

Follow-up:

The patient was told to come back to the clinic for more tests and care.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Patient ID: [ID]
Date of Admission: [Date of admission]
Date of Discharge: [Date of discharge]

Admitting Diagnosis: A spinal cord disease called HAM caused by a virus (HTLV-I) that developed after a kidney transplant

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 65-year-old man. He had kidney disease caused by diabetes. He received a kidney transplant from his wife. His wife carried a virus called HTLV-I in her blood. Eight months after the transplant, the patient's legs became weak. The weakness got worse very quickly. Within 12 days, he needed a wheelchair to move around. He was given high doses of steroids, but his leg strength did not come back. He was then moved to our hospital.

At our hospital, doctors checked his nervous system. His legs were weak and floppy. His reflex responses were lower than normal. Tests on his nerves showed they were working fine. Blood tests showed he had the HTLV-I virus. Fluid from his spine had too much protein and too many cells. Tests confirmed the virus was in his spinal fluid.

Scans of his middle back showed signs of swelling and damage in his spinal cord. Based on all these findings, doctors diagnosed him with HAM. This is a spinal cord disease caused by the HTLV-I virus. The patient started treatment with a medicine called interferon-alpha. This did not help much. Doctors then added another treatment that uses antibodies from donated blood. This is called IVIg. After getting both treatments together, the patient got better. He was able to move his legs more easily. Later scans showed his spinal cord had gotten smaller. His ability to move improved during his hospital stay.

Discharge Condition:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition. He should keep seeing his regular doctor and brain and nerve specialist. He should keep taking interferon-alpha and IVIg at his follow-up visits. He should also keep going to physical therapy to help him move better.

Summary:

A 65-year-old man had kidney disease from diabetes and received a kidney transplant. He developed weak and floppy legs. Doctors found he had a spinal cord disease called HAM caused by the HTLV-I virus. He was treated with interferon-alpha and IVIg. He got better and left the hospital in stable condition. He will continue to see his doctors for follow-up care.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Low calcium levels in the blood and a full-body seizure with shaking and stiffness

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with a new full-body seizure with shaking and stiffness. A physical exam showed the patient had short height, wide-set eyes, droopy upper eyelids, a large forehead, a nasal-sounding voice, and a wide nose bridge. Blood tests showed very low calcium levels. More tests found that the parathyroid glands were not working well. The patient also had some unusual facial features. Because of this, doctors did genetic testing. The tests found a missing piece of genetic material linked to DiGeorge syndrome. The patient was given calcium citrate and calcitriol to raise calcium levels. After treatment, the patient had no more symptoms and calcium levels returned to normal. A heart ultrasound, belly ultrasound, and brain wave test were all normal. A brain scan showed calcium buildup in a deep part of the brain called the basal ganglia.

Hospital Course:
A 65-year-old woman came to the hospital for red, scaly, itchy patches on her arms and legs. She also had flaky skin on her scalp and behind her ears. The patient was being treated with a cancer drug called nivolumab every 2 weeks. She had received this drug 11 times before coming to the hospital. Two years ago, she was told she had advanced skin cancer called melanoma. This cancer had spread to her lymph nodes, the tissue under her skin, and her brain. The cancer had a specific change in a gene called BRAF V600. Nivolumab was her third cancer treatment after two other drugs called a BRAF blocker and ipilimumab.

The patient already had a history of scalp psoriasis, which is a skin condition that causes scaly patches. She also had type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. Her regular medicines included lorametazepam, gliclazide, metoprolol, pantoprazole, and mometasone nasal spray. Doctors checked her whole body and found no other skin problems. The patient felt well overall. She had no weight loss, night sweats, fever, trouble breathing, cough, or stomach problems.

Based on her symptoms, doctors found that her psoriasis had gotten worse. They started treating the skin patches with steroid cream. They also changed her nivolumab schedule from every 2 weeks to every 3 weeks. The patient had noticed her skin got worse after each nivolumab dose. The longer time between doses plus the steroid cream helped control the skin patches. The patient did not need steroid pills or shots.

The patient's cancer stayed stable for 14 months after starting nivolumab. Then the cancer in her brain grew worse and caused bleeding inside her head. The patient died from this.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Worsening of psoriasis, a skin condition that causes red, scaly patches.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. Her skin symptoms got better with steroid cream and nivolumab doses every 3 weeks. The patient was told to see her cancer doctor for ongoing care of her advanced melanoma. No other visits to this hospital are needed.

Recommended Follow-up:
The patient should see her cancer doctor for ongoing care of her advanced melanoma.

The 28-year-old female patient has a history of a condition where certain white blood cells cause stomach and intestine swelling. On the next day after the procedure, the patient developed fever, yellowing of the skin, confusion, and belly pain. She was diagnosed with a serious infection of the bile ducts. The patient's condition has improved a lot, and she is stable enough to go home. The bulge had shrunk a lot and now measured 53 by 53 mm. The patient showed no signs of infection when this report was written.

Diagnosis:
Bulge in the lower part of the main artery

Procedures:
Repair of the artery bulge using a tube inserted through a blood vessel

Condition at Discharge:
The patient left the hospital without serious problems.

Follow-Up:
A scan was done 15 months after the repair. The bulge had shrunk a lot. The patient had stopped taking antibiotics when this report was written.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient name]
Date of Admission: [Date]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course Summary:

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a healthy 3.5-year-old boy. The patient was admitted because of weakness and pale skin for five days. Two weeks before coming to the hospital, the patient had loose stools for three days. A physical exam showed yellow skin, pale skin, and an enlarged spleen. Blood tests showed low red blood cell levels. The blood sample also showed unusual red blood cells. The patient was diagnosed with a condition where the body attacks its own red blood cells. This is called warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Hospital Course:
The patient received a blood transfusion. The patient then received a strong steroid medicine through an IV. The patient responded very well to this treatment. The patient took steroid pills for four weeks. The dose was slowly lowered over the next five months. The patient got sick again after catching a cold. The steroid pills were restarted and worked well. When the dose was lowered, the blood counts got worse again. A medicine called azathioprine was started. The blood counts got a little worse. After the parents agreed in writing, a medicine called rituximab was started. The patient received four doses, one each week. Two months later, the patient was doing well. After 12 months, blood tests showed the condition was gone. The patient has been healthy with no return of the illness for three years.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, a condition where the body attacks its own red blood cells

Discharge Medication:
None

Discharge Condition:
Stable

Follow-up Appointments:
The patient should see the right doctors as needed.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should eat healthy foods and get enough rest.

Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. This is when the body attacks its own red blood cells. The patient was treated with blood transfusions and several medicines. These included steroids given by IV and by mouth, azathioprine, and rituximab. The patient responded well to treatment. The patient has been healthy with no return of the illness for three years.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 35-year-old Hispanic male. He has a history of AIDS, Kaposi sarcoma (a type of cancer), and Castleman's disease (a condition that causes swollen lymph nodes). He came to the hospital with severe on-and-off pain in his middle to lower back. The pain spread to both legs over the past week. The patient also had numbness in his legs and trouble moving.

Admission Note:
When the patient arrived, he had a fever of 38.5 degrees Celsius. His heart was beating faster than normal. The doctor's exam found swollen lymph nodes throughout the body. Both legs had swelling that did not leave a dent when pressed. The patient had a drooping right eyelid and one side of the face was drooping. The skin showed dark purple and red raised spots on both thighs. These spots are signs of Kaposi sarcoma.

Diagnostic Findings:
Blood tests showed low platelet counts and low protein levels. Imaging scans showed an enlarged liver. The scans also showed swollen lymph nodes in the belly and pelvis area. Swollen lymph nodes were also found above the collarbones, under the arms, in the chest, and along the spine. MRI scans confirmed these findings.

Consultations:
The infection specialists suggested HIV treatment with Raltegravir 400 mg tablet twice a day. They also suggested Abacavir and Lamivudine 600 and 300 mg tablet once a day. The blood and cancer specialists wanted to check for a type of blood cancer. They suggested a bone marrow test and removal of a lymph node above the collarbone for testing. A brain MRI and a spinal fluid test were also done.

Procedures:
The removed lymph node from above the left collarbone showed Kaposi sarcoma. It also showed Castleman's disease. The bone marrow test showed the marrow was making more cells than usual. It showed a reaction in the immune cells but no cancer in the bone marrow.

Treatment:
The patient went home in stable condition. The patient was taking HIV medicines. The patient had follow-up visits scheduled with the infection and cancer doctors. The patient received cancer treatment called CHOP as an outpatient. CHOP includes cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine, and prednisone. This was given once a month for four months. The patient also received rituximab and medicine to prevent a lung infection. The drooping eyelid and face drooping got better during treatment. The swollen lymph nodes went away after finishing all the treatment.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was told to follow up with the infection specialists and cancer doctors. They will continue to manage care as an outpatient.

Summary:
A 35-year-old patient came in with middle to lower back pain. The patient was found to have Kaposi sarcoma, a type of cancer. The patient received treatment and went home in stable condition after finishing cancer treatment. The patient should follow up with the infection specialists and cancer doctors.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 25-year-old man from Iraq. He came to the hospital with painful lumps under his skin, trouble walking, and repeated high fevers. He has long-term kidney disease and needs dialysis two times a week to clean his blood. He had a kidney transplant in the past, but his body rejected it. Doctors had to remove the transplanted kidney. He was treated before for a lung infection called tuberculosis. He also had a liver infection called hepatitis C. He took medicine called interferon for this, but it was stopped because his blood cell counts dropped too low.

Diagnostic Assessment:
The physical exam showed lumps under his skin. His joints were stiff and hard to move. He had painful sores that were hard and swollen. Blood tests showed low red blood cells, low white blood cells, and low platelets. His kidney waste levels were high. His calcium and phosphorus levels were not normal. A hormone that controls calcium was very high. His vitamin D level was normal. A liver enzyme was high. Aluminum levels in his urine were high. A bone scan showed calcium buildup in places it should not be. A CT scan also showed calcium buildup in soft body tissues.

Diagnosis and Management:
The patient was diagnosed with tumoral calcinosis. This means calcium lumps formed in his body tissues. He was treated with dialysis fluid that has less calcium. He took a medicine called Sevelemer to lower phosphorus. He also got treatment to remove extra aluminum from his body. After eight dialysis sessions, his fever went down and his joint pain got better. He was sent home to continue treatment in his hometown.

Follow-Up and Recommendations:
The patient should keep using low-calcium dialysis fluid and phosphorus-lowering medicine. He should see his kidney doctor for regular checkups. He should drink enough fluids. He should eat foods low in calcium and phosphorus. He should not take antacids or medicines that contain aluminum. He should avoid activities that could hurt or put pressure on the affected areas. He should see a doctor right away if he notices any new symptoms.

Blood tests showed her white blood cell count was very low at 830, far below normal. A chest x-ray and CT scan showed a small area of infection in her left lung.

Medical History:
The patient has a history of irregular heartbeat, stroke, high blood pressure, weak bladder, lower back pain, and stomach irritation.

Medications:
The patient was taking several daily medications. DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 8
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient came to the hospital because of belly pain. The pain got better with basic care. Six years ago, he was found to have a blood vessel problem he was born with. This problem causes blood to flow around the liver instead of through it. He also takes medicine for trouble focusing and staying still.

Blood tests showed high ammonia levels in his blood. His blood was also not clotting the way it should. Scans showed the blood vessel problem and a growth in his liver.

The patient's parents chose to watch the condition closely instead of doing a procedure right away. But six months later, his ammonia levels went up a lot. The amount of blood going around his liver had also increased. This meant he could have brain problems from the high ammonia. So, doctors did a procedure through a blood vessel to close off the problem area.

During the procedure, the patient had some bleeding where the tube went in. Doctors stopped it quickly by pressing on the area while watching with an ultrasound. Within six days, his ammonia levels dropped back to normal. He went home after nine days.

FOLLOW-UP:

Two weeks after the procedure, a belly ultrasound showed the problem areas were closed. The liver growth had also gotten smaller. Blood flow to the right side of the liver had increased a lot. The spleen had grown just a little. A scan one month later showed the blood vessel problem was fully fixed. Blood was flowing better to the right side of the liver. The liver growth was almost completely gone.

When the patient left the hospital, he was doing well and thinking clearly. His body check and heart rate, breathing, and temperature were all normal. His medicines were reviewed. He was told to see his regular doctor for follow-up.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

1. A blood vessel problem present from birth that makes blood flow around the liver.
2. A growth in the liver.

DISCHARGE PLAN:

1. See the regular doctor for checkups and ongoing care.
2. Keep taking all medicines as before.
3. The patient can eat all foods with no limits.
4. No hard exercise or rough play for two weeks.
5. Come back to the hospital if there are any worries or problems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Patient's name]
Age: 60-year-old male
Medical history: None

Admission:
The patient was sent to the Urology Department after doctors found a growth on the left kidney by chance. Doctors also found spots on the liver. A physical exam showed a lump in the upper left belly area. The lump could be moved and was slightly painful. Blood tests showed high levels of certain liver enzymes called alkaline phosphatase, GGT, and LDH. Tests showed that hormone levels from the adrenal glands were normal in blood and urine. An ultrasound of the belly showed a growth on the left kidney and several spots on the liver. A CT scan showed several small spots on the lungs. It also showed a growth on the left adrenal gland with no clear signs of spreading into nearby tissue.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for planned surgery. The diagnosis was cancer of the left adrenal gland. The cancer had formed a blood clot in the left kidney vein. It had also spread to the liver and lungs. Doctors made a cut across both sides of the upper belly to remove the blood clot caused by the tumor. The surgical team fully separated and removed the tumor blood clot. Doctors removed the left adrenal vein but saved the kidney on the same side. Doctors also removed nearby lymph nodes. Kidney function tests were normal and there were no problems after surgery. The patient is now taking a medicine called mitotane. The dose is being slowly increased.

Diagnosis:
Cancer of the adrenal gland measuring 15 cm by 6 cm by 11 cm. A tumor blood clot in the left kidney vein measuring 4 cm by 2 cm by 1 cm.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will continue treatment with two cancer-fighting medicines called adriamycin and cisplatin.
