Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Age: 14 years
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Discharge Diagnosis: A non-cancerous sac filled with skin-like tissue near the lower end of the spinal cord

Hospital Course:

The patient was first told he had a spine infection called tuberculosis by a local doctor. He was given medicine for that illness. But the patient got worse, so he was moved to our hospital. He had pain in his lower back. He also had weakness and numbness in both legs. The patient's thinking and memory were normal. The nerves in his head and face were working fine.

Doctors found that the muscles in both lower legs had gotten smaller. The left side had loose muscle tone. Both legs had weak strength, rated 3 out of 5. Reflexes were missing in both legs. The patient had reduced feeling in parts of his right leg. He could not feel light touch or sharp pokes as well as normal. Feeling was also reduced in the area around his buttocks and upper thighs.

Scans showed a small, clearly shaped growth measuring about 1.5 by 0.6 centimeters. This growth was inside the spinal canal and pressing on the lower end of the spinal cord. The growth was located at the middle-to-lower back area. It had clear edges and different shades on the scan images.

Doctors did surgery through a straight cut in the middle of the back. They found the spinal cord was being squeezed by a growth inside it. They made a small opening in the spinal cord covering. Inside, they found a grayish-white sac with one pocket. This sac was growing in the lower end of the spinal cord. The doctors drained the sac and removed almost all of it. Lab tests showed the sac was a harmless cyst lined with skin cells.

After surgery, the patient slowly got stronger. Leg strength improved to 4 out of 5. Feeling for light touch and sharp pokes came back. One month later, the patient had no nerve problems. He could move around and walk with help.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged on [REDACTED]. Please follow up with your primary care doctor or brain and nerve specialist for further consultation. In case of any return of symptoms, please return to our hospital immediately.

Signed,

Admitting Diagnosis: Uterus slipping down into the vagina (second stage)

Chief Complaint: Occasional vaginal bleeding

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the hospital at 28 weeks of pregnancy. She had occasional vaginal bleeding. Doctors found that her uterus had slipped down into the vagina (second stage). An exam showed the lowest part of the uterus had dropped down. An ultrasound showed her cervix was short at 17 mm and shaped like a T. She was given a hormone capsule to place in the vagina each day.

Two weeks later, at 30 weeks of pregnancy, the patient came back. She was having regular tightening of the uterus. Her cervix was now even shorter at 10 mm. Doctors gave her medicine to stop early labor, and it worked well. She also received medicine to help the baby's lungs develop faster. The patient was told to stay in bed with her feet slightly higher than her head. A test found a vaginal infection. It was treated with a single dose of azithromycin 1,000 mg.

At 34 weeks of pregnancy, the tightening stopped without medicine. The patient went home. She came back at 37 weeks because the tightening started again. Her cervix was still slipping down and had opened to about 3 cm. After a waiting period, she gave birth to a healthy baby boy. She lost about 400 mL of blood, which is normal for childbirth. The baby scored 10 out of 10 on health tests at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth.

The doctor gently pushed the uterus back into place by hand. Recovery after birth went smoothly. Two days after giving birth, the patient went home in good health. Her cervix was no longer slipping down. Checkups at 1 month and 6 months after birth showed no signs of the uterus slipping down.

Slowly return to normal activities as the patient feels able.
Talk to a healthcare provider about keeping the vaginal area clean.
Get medical help right away if vaginal bleeding or unusual discharge happens.
Take all prescribed medicines as directed.
Eat healthy foods and exercise regularly.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 44
Gender: Female
Main Problem: Painful mouth sore

Hospital Stay:
The patient came to the hospital with a painful mouth sore that started 6 weeks before. She had a history of recurring mouth sores and was given steroid medicine that works throughout the body. Her condition got worse and she developed a red, bumpy rash on her body. She also had red eyes, fever, loose stools, and lost weight. Blood tests showed high levels of white blood cells and a type of white blood cell called eosinophils. Doctors thought she might have Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, a serious skin reaction. She was treated with steroids that work throughout the body. Her skin got a little better but her mouth sores did not improve.
A small sample of skin was tested and showed damage where the skin layers meet. It also showed blisters forming under the top skin layer. These findings matched a condition called paraneoplastic pemphigus. More tests showed that her immune system was attacking normal skin and organ tissue. The patient was finally found to have stage IV follicular lymphoma, a type of blood cancer that had spread. She also had a lung condition called bronchiolitis obliterans and a serious fungal lung infection called invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
Cancer treatment led to complete disappearance of the lymphoma. This was confirmed through a special imaging scan that detects cancer activity. The patient's mouth sores and skin rash stayed under control with a low dose of steroid medicine for 8 months. However, she developed the lung condition and serious fungal lung infection. These caused her lungs to stop working.

Treatment Given:
Treatment included cancer-fighting drugs called rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone. These medicines led to complete disappearance of the patient's lymphoma. The patient also took a low dose of steroid medicine at 5mg per day. This kept her mouth sores and skin rash under control.

Follow-Up Care:
No follow-up care is needed because the patient died from lung failure.

Diagnosis:
The patient was found to have paraneoplastic pemphigus, a rare skin blistering disease. This was linked to stage IV follicular lymphoma, a blood cancer that had spread. She also had bronchiolitis obliterans, a lung condition, and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, a serious fungal lung infection.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 43-year-old male, was admitted to our Kidney Unit for trouble breathing and fever. He was diagnosed with a type of kidney disease called membranous glomerulonephritis along with long-term kidney disease that did not need dialysis. The patient was being treated with two medicines called cyclophosphamide and prednisone.

At the time of admission, the patient had a fever and trouble breathing with low oxygen levels at 86.7%. Listening to the chest showed crackling sounds and less air moving through the lungs. A blood test showed the lungs were not getting enough oxygen into the blood. The patient had a detailed scan of the chest, which showed patchy cloudy areas in both lungs. The patient was diagnosed with a serious lung condition where the lungs fill with fluid.

The patient was treated with medicines to fight infection including piperacillin/tazobactam, levofloxacin, and fluconazole. A breathing machine that pushes air into the lungs was started when the patient's breathing got worse. The patient's health got worse, causing an irregular heartbeat and higher levels of waste products in the blood. Because the condition was so serious, a blood cleaning treatment called CPFA was started.

The patient had three days in a row of CPFA blood cleaning treatment. Levels of substances that cause swelling and infection were checked before and after each treatment. The patient's health improved quickly, and the breathing machine was removed 24 hours after the first CPFA treatment. The patient was no longer confused and the heartbeat returned to normal. After four days, the patient's oxygen level was 97% while breathing regular air.

The patient's illness severity score went down from 24 to 9, and a follow-up chest scan was done after nine days. This scan showed the lung problem had improved a lot.

Discharge Summary:

The patient, a 43-year-old male with a history of a kidney disease called membranous glomerulonephritis, was admitted to our unit for a serious lung condition. The patient received treatment with medicines to fight infection and a breathing machine. Also, blood cleaning treatment was started and used for three days in a row, which helped the patient get better.

At the time of discharge, the patient's illness severity score was 9, the oxygen level was 97% while breathing regular air, and a follow-up chest scan showed the lung problem had improved a lot. The patient was sent home from our unit in stable condition. Patients were advised to follow-up with their kidney specialist for ongoing care and management of their kidney disease.

Diagnosis:
Pyoderma gangrenosum of the penis. This is a rare skin condition that causes painful sores.

The patient was given a steroid medicine called prednisone. The pain got much better within a few days.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 38-year-old male, came to the clinic for repeated skin infections near the tailbone. Initial blood tests showed a high white blood cell count (18700/L) with 64% of one type called lymphocytes. A closer look at the blood confirmed too many lymphocytes. More tests were done to rule out blood cancer.

A special blood test was done to find out why the lymphocyte count stayed high. The test showed three different groups of cells. The largest group was lymphocytes. Many of these cells did not fit into the usual groups of immune cells. More testing showed these cells were natural killer cells, making up 43% of all cells tested. The diagnosis was a condition where natural killer cells grow too much. This is called chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK cells (CLPD-NK).

During his stay, the patient was watched closely. His condition was checked often. Based on test results, the doctors confirmed he had CLPD-NK.

The patient received care to support his health. His condition got better over time. He handled the hospital stay well and had no major problems. The patient left the hospital in stable condition. He was told how to care for and prevent more skin infections. He was also told to see his regular doctor to keep track of his high lymphocyte count.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Too many natural killer cells in the blood, known as chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK cells (CLPD-NK)

Discharge Instructions:

1. Take all prescribed medicines as your regular doctor tells you.
2. Stay healthy by eating balanced meals and exercising regularly.
3. Stay away from people who are sick with infections.
4. Wash your hands well and keep clean to prevent more skin infections.
5. See your regular doctor for checkups to monitor your high lymphocyte count.

Follow-Up:

The patient should make an appointment with his regular doctor within two weeks after leaving the hospital. More blood tests may be needed to check if the lymphocyte count changes and to make sure treatment is working.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Generalized Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption (GBFDE), a serious skin reaction to medicine
Final Diagnosis: Generalized Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption (GBFDE), a serious skin reaction to medicine

Hospital Course:
A 24-year-old male came to the hospital with red skin all over the body. The patient also had fluid-filled blisters on the chest, back, stomach, arms, and legs. Before this happened, the patient had taken several medicines. These included cetirizine for allergies, paracetamol for pain, and pseudoephedrine for congestion. The patient said this had happened 4-5 times before. Each time, the reaction was worse than the time before. The patient was given a medicine called cyclosporine. The blisters healed within 5-7 days but left lighter-colored patches on the skin. The patient left the hospital in good health.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Generalized Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption (GBFDE). This is a rare and serious skin reaction to certain medicines. It causes skin cells to die and form blisters that separate from deeper skin layers. Some medicines, like cetirizine, can cause the body's defense system to overreact. This leads to widespread blisters and raw, open skin areas.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with cyclosporine. This medicine blocks a chemical in the body called interleukin-2 (IL-2). By doing this, it calms down certain white blood cells that attack the skin. It also stops a process that causes skin cells to die. Cyclosporine works better for this condition than steroid medicines or treatments given through a vein.

Follow-Up:
Six months later, the patient took a paracetamol pill for a fever. The healed skin areas became very painful and red again. This proved that paracetamol was causing the GBFDE skin reaction.

Prognosis:
Doctors used to think GBFDE was not very dangerous. However, a study compared 58 patients with GBFDE to patients with similar skin conditions called SJS/TEN. The study found that death rates were almost the same in both groups. This means GBFDE can be just as serious as SJS/TEN. Severe cases of GBFDE need fast and effective treatment.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was told to stay away from medicines that could cause this skin reaction again. The patient was also told to see their regular doctor if any symptoms come back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient 261 is a 40-year-old woman. She had blood in her urine and protein in her urine during pregnancy. She came to the hospital to check on her kidney problems. No one in her family has had kidney disease or hearing loss.

Doctors did gene testing to learn more about her condition. The tests found two harmful changes in her genes. One change was in a gene called COL4A4. The other change was in a gene called CFH. These gene changes point to a type of inherited kidney disease.

While in the hospital, doctors checked her blood pressure often. She had high blood pressure during pregnancy, but it went away after she gave birth. However, protein kept showing up in her urine. This happened even though she took medicine to protect her kidneys. Doctors took a small sample of her kidney tissue to look at it closely. They found that the thin layer in her kidneys was too thin. They also found some hardening of her blood vessels. Some small blood vessel damage was present. Two out of ten filtering units in her kidneys had scarring.

Doctors followed her health for 60 months. Her kidneys kept working well during this time. Her overall health stayed good. She still has protein and blood in her urine, but her condition is stable. Her parents could not be tested.

In summary, Patient 261 has a thin layer in her kidneys that causes blood in her urine. This is due to the harmful change in the COL4A4 gene. She also has low levels of a blood protein called C3 because of the CFH gene change. She takes medicine to protect her kidneys. Doctors watch her blood pressure and kidney function closely. Her kidneys have stayed stable. She will keep seeing her regular doctor and kidney specialist for ongoing care.

Hospital Course:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Chief Complaint: Unable to get pregnant

History of Present Illness:
The patient was a 37-year-old Korean woman who had irregular periods and trouble getting pregnant. She was sent to the fertility clinic at this hospital for treatment. The patient had previously given birth to a baby with a rare condition where the body does not respond normally to male hormones. That child had surgery to repair bulges in the groin area on both sides. The patient had no problems with growth or development. She had no family history of diabetes or heart disease.

Past Medical History:
The patient had a history of irregular periods and trouble getting pregnant. She had a body mass index of 22.1, which is in the normal weight range. She also had extra body hair growth, rated as mild on a standard scale.

Physical Examination:
The physical exam showed no problems with growth or development. No problems with the female reproductive organs were found.

Diagnostic Assessment:
The patient had an ultrasound and a CT scan of the belly and pelvis area. The scans showed that both male sex glands were present in the groin areas on both sides. The womb, birth canal, and egg-producing organs were not seen on the scan. The patient was diagnosed with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. This is a condition where the body does not respond to male hormones at all. Genetic testing of the hormone receptor gene was done. The results showed the patient carries the gene for this condition. Blood tests showed high levels of a hormone that measures egg supply. Male hormone levels were also higher than normal. An internal ultrasound showed the egg-producing organs had many small fluid-filled sacs. The patient was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome.

Hospital Course:
The patient received fertility treatment. This included testing embryos for genetic conditions before placing them in the womb.

Discharge medications:
None

Follow-up instructions:
The patient was told to see her doctor for ongoing care and regular check-ups.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name]
DOB: [Date of Birth]
MRN: [Medical Record Number]
Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]

Diagnosis:
Retinitis pigmentosa (a condition that damages the back of the eye and affects vision)
Intermittent diplopia (double vision that comes and goes)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with double vision that had been happening on and off for a few years. The double vision had recently gotten worse. An eye doctor looked at the back of the patient's eyes. The exam showed damage to the light-sensing tissue, narrowed blood vessels, and pale nerve areas in both eyes. This led to a diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa. A vision field test showed the patient could only see in a small central area in both eyes. Eye alignment tests showed the left eye was higher than it should be and turned slightly outward. The muscles that move the left eye were not working properly. The patient tried special glasses with prisms that stopped the double vision. However, the patient did not want to wear these glasses and asked for surgery instead.

The patient had surgery to fix a muscle in the left eye. This helped improve the eye alignment. One month after surgery, the left eye was still slightly higher and turned outward. The patient only had double vision when looking up and to the right. There was no double vision when looking straight ahead or at close objects. At a check-up three months later, the eye measurements were the same. The patient was happy because the double vision no longer bothered daily activities.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will have regular check-ups with an eye doctor. These visits will track any changes in the eye condition. The doctor will also check if double vision comes back in the future.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 39-year-old woman with a blood cancer called multiple myeloma, which affects certain cells in the bone marrow

Hospital Course:

The patient came to our hospital in January 2011 with multiple myeloma at an advanced stage. She received four rounds of cancer treatment with three drugs called bortezomib, adriamycin, and dexamethasone. She also got a bone-strengthening medicine called zoledronic acid. In August 2011, the patient had a transplant using her own stem cells collected from her blood. Before this transplant, she received a strong chemotherapy drug called melphalan to prepare her body. In March 2013, the cancer came back and caused one of her spine bones to collapse. The patient then started treatment with two different drugs called lenalidomide and dexamethasone. After four rounds, this treatment stopped working well. The patient then received a different set of three drugs called bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone. This treatment worked and the cancer went away completely for the second time. In December 2013, the patient received stem cells from a sibling whose cells were a perfect match. This transplant used a gentler preparation treatment to support her good response. In April 2014, the cancer returned in the bone marrow and also formed a tumor in the shin bone. The patient again received bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone. This treatment was stopped after two rounds because bortezomib caused nerve damage in the hands and feet. The patient then started a different combination of cancer drugs including vincristine, carmustine, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, prednisone, and doxorubicin with high-dose dexamethasone. This treatment worked and the cancer went away completely for the third time.

In April 2015, the patient had fluid buildup around the heart that was pressing on it dangerously. Doctors drained the fluid with a needle and this problem went away. In May 2015, the patient had a large amount of fluid buildup around the left lung. Doctors drained this fluid twice and found cancer cells in it. Even though the cancer had spread to this new area, tests of the blood, urine, and bone marrow showed no signs of cancer. The patient then started treatment with two drugs called carfilzomib and dexamethasone. The patient quickly felt much better and left the hospital with no more fluid around the lung.

Follow-Up Recommendations:

The patient is now on the 18th round of treatment and the cancer remains gone 19 months after it spread outside the bone marrow. The patient will have more appointments scheduled to check on her health.

Discharge Summary:

Patient ID: [insert patient ID]
Name: [insert patient name]
Age: 47
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [insert admission date]
Discharge Date: [insert discharge date]

Diagnosis:
The patient has an aggressive brain cancer called glioblastoma in the left front part of the brain. The cancer has come back.

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with trouble speaking and memory problems. A brain scan showed a 4-centimeter fluid-filled tumor with swelling in the left front part of the brain. Doctors removed part of the tumor through surgery. Lab tests confirmed it was an aggressive brain cancer. After surgery, the patient received radiation and a cancer drug called TMZ at the same time. Six months after the first surgery, the patient's symptoms got worse. A new brain scan showed the cancer had come back. Doctors used a focused radiation treatment called Gamma Knife to treat the returned cancer. The patient also received a drug called BEV through an IV every two weeks. The patient kept taking TMZ as well. After two months of treatment with both BEV and TMZ, the cancer was no longer visible. The patient stayed in stable health, and brain scans showed no cancer growth. Seventeen months after starting BEV, the cancer came back again. The patient continued visits at our clinic. Twenty-two months after finishing BEV treatment, a brain scan showed the cancer had spread quickly. Multiple tumors were now found on both sides of the brain.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's condition is very serious. More treatments are needed to help manage the patient's symptoms.

Recommendations:
The patient should continue regular doctor visits and treatment to manage symptoms. Doctors should look at other treatment options to address the cancer that has returned and spread.

Hospital Course:
The 31-year-old male patient was admitted because his vision had been getting more blurry for 3 weeks. A brain scan showed several fluid-filled sacs in an area at the base of the brain. A spinal tap was done to collect fluid from around the spine. The test showed higher than normal pressure, more white blood cells than normal, higher protein, and lower sugar. The spinal fluid also showed more of a type of white blood cell linked to parasites. Tests for fungal infection and tuberculosis in the spinal fluid came back negative. Special DNA testing of the spinal fluid found signs of a pork tapeworm. Blood and spinal fluid tests also showed signs that the body was fighting this tapeworm infection. The patient was told he had a tapeworm infection at the base of the brain. He was treated with a medicine to kill parasites, a medicine to reduce swelling, and a procedure to drain fluid from the brain. The patient's symptoms and spinal fluid test results got much better after treatment.

Tapeworm infection at the base of the brain.

A medicine to kill parasites, a medicine to reduce swelling, and a procedure to drain fluid from the brain were given.

The patient should keep taking all medicines and follow all care steps as told by the doctor. The patient should not eat raw or undercooked pork or drink water that may be dirty. The patient should get medical help right away if any new symptoms appear or if current symptoms get worse.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Patient Name: [Patient Name]                Medical Record Number: [Medical Record Number]

Reason for admission: Sudden kidney damage and liver swelling with blocked bile flow
Final diagnosis: Long-term liver disease caused by both hepatitis C virus and the body's immune system attacking itself

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 55-year-old woman with both HIV and hepatitis C virus (type 3a) found in 1991. The patient also has a history of injecting drugs. The patient had been taking HIV medicines since 1991, and these worked well. In 2005, the hepatitis C came back after 24 weeks of treatment with two medicines called pegIFN and ribavirin. In 2007, the patient had two episodes of sudden kidney damage along with liver swelling and blocked bile flow. The patient needed to stay in the hospital. The HIV medicines were stopped. The patient received blood filtering treatment, a protein called albumin, vitamin K, and blood products. The patient started a steroid medicine called methylprednisolone and went home taking steroid pills.

Three months later, the patient came back to the hospital with new sudden kidney damage. Doctors took a small sample of kidney tissue to study. It showed swelling in the kidney tubes and scarring in the kidney filters. The steroid medicine methylprednisolone was restarted and worked well. The patient went home taking prednisone pills, and the dose was slowly lowered over time. In January 2008, the kidney doctor suggested stopping the steroid and starting a medicine called mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) for long-term care. The patient restarted HIV medicines along with MMF. A blood test for certain antibodies that attack smooth muscle came back negative. The patient stayed on MMF until November 2009 when it was stopped. The liver and kidneys got worse again, so MMF had to be restarted. Over the next few years, the patient stayed on MMF while changing HIV medicines.

In June 2012, the liver swelling with blocked bile flow happened again. The patient did not want to take steroid medicines anymore. So the doctors raised the MMF dose instead. The patient continued this higher dose in the following years, and the kidney and liver test results got better. In September 2015, the patient took two hepatitis C medicines called sofosbuvir and daclatasvir for 12 weeks. The patient did not need ribavirin this time. The hepatitis C virus was cleared from the body and stayed gone. MMF was then slowly lowered and stopped. Later blood tests showed the hepatitis C virus stayed gone. The kidney waste product levels and liver test results stayed normal. The antibodies that attack smooth muscle stayed negative 12 months after stopping MMF. The patient started taking a single combined HIV pill.

Laboratory Data:

Blood tests showed sudden kidney failure. The waste product level in the blood was very high at 6.3 mg/dL. Other waste products in the blood were also high. Test results also showed too much of a yellow substance called bilirubin in the blood, liver failure, blood that did not clot well, and too much acid in the blood. A test for antibodies that attack smooth muscle was positive. Tests for many other types of antibodies that attack the body were negative. These included antibodies that attack cell centers, antibodies that attack proteins attached to genetic material, antibodies that attack fatty substances, antibodies that attack certain white blood cells, antibodies that attack the outer layer of the kidney glands, antibodies that attack energy makers in cells, and antibodies that attack liver and kidney tissue. Urine tests showed protein, blood, and pus in the urine. A sound wave picture of the belly showed a larger than normal liver without any masses. There was a small amount of fluid in the belly. The kidneys were larger than normal and had higher blood flow resistance.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient left the hospital in good health. The patient should see their kidney doctor, liver doctor, and infection disease doctor for follow-up visits. The patient should keep taking their HIV medicines as directed. The patient should go to all regular check-up appointments.

Hospital Course:

In this hospital course, a 43-year-old male came in with pain in his penis during sex. The patient also reported months of headaches that came and went with no signs of nerve problems. When doctors looked at his private parts, they found three shallow sores on the top side of his penis. The sores were removed through surgery. Lab tests showed the sores were round, enclosed growths made of twisted bundles of long, thin cells. These cells tested positive for certain proteins called vimentin and S-100. The features of these growths matched a diagnosis of penile schwannomas. Schwannomas are harmless tumors that grow from the covering of nerves.

A nerve specialist was asked to look into the patient's headache on the side of his head. The exam found no signs of nerve problems. A brain and spine scan using magnets and radio waves was then done. The scan showed a small, round growth at the top of the bundle of nerves at the base of the spine. This growth was at the level between the first and second lower back bones. The growth lit up along its full length on the scan. It looked like it was growing from a nerve root at that spot. The rest of the scan looked normal. The features of this growth matched a spinal schwannoma. Doctors chose to watch the growth with regular scans because it was small. The patient's symptoms were also mild and not causing major problems.

The patient was watched for two years after the first diagnosis. The growth has stayed the same size. The patient did not report any new symptoms.

Condition on Discharge:

The patient was not admitted to the hospital and was not discharged. The patient is currently being watched and cared for through regular scans.

Impression:

1. Penile schwannomas, which are harmless nerve tumors on the penis
2. Spinal schwannoma, which is a harmless nerve tumor on the spine

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for a surgery to remove the prostate using a robotic system. The patient was put to sleep with general anesthesia. No problems were reported during the surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with variant angina. This is a type of chest pain caused by a sudden tightening of the heart's blood vessels.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 76-year-old man had robotic surgery to remove his prostate. He was put to sleep with general anesthesia and received no calming medicine beforehand. During surgery, his heart started beating in an abnormal pattern. This led to his heart stopping, and the medical team performed CPR to restart it. After his heart was restarted, doctors found he had variant angina. The patient was moved to the intensive care unit for close watching. He received medicines called dopamine and norepinephrine through an IV to support his heart and blood pressure. Doctors did a test to look at the blood vessels in his heart. They found blockages in two arteries, the right coronary artery and the left circumflex artery. A special test also showed that his blood vessels were having spasms. The breathing tube was removed on day 1 after surgery. The patient left the hospital on day 8 after surgery without any problems. His heart test and blood work were normal at that time. Four weeks after leaving the hospital, the patient had a skin test. The test checked for a reaction to two medicines used during surgery. The test came back negative, meaning no reaction was found.

Disposition:
The patient was sent home.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was in stable condition.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary

Patient name: [insert name]
Admission date: [insert date]
Discharge date: [insert date]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 58-year-old male worker. He came in with a rough, scaly patch of skin on his right lower back. The patch started as a small ring-shaped spot. It grew outward into a larger patch. The patch stayed the same size for seven years. Then it started spreading again in the last two years. The patient often worked without a shirt for long hours. He felt itching and burning in hot weather.

Investigations:
The patients had many tests done. All test results came back normal. The patients tested negative for HIV. Their immune systems were working well. Doctors thought the skin problem was porokeratosis. A skin sample test confirmed this. The sample showed special features in the skin layers that matched this condition.

Treatment:
The patients were told to wear clothes that protect from the sun. They were given isotretinoin 20mg pills to take by mouth. They were also given halobetasol 0.05% cream to put on the skin at night. The patient with itching and burning in the sun had part of the patch removed. He also had freezing treatment. After that, he put on tretinoin 0.05% cream and fluorouracil 5% cream on different nights. This patient had side effects every 3-4 weeks. These included redness, itching, oozing, crusting, and swelling. After five months, the skin showed fair improvement.

Follow-up:
One of the three patients stopped coming to appointments. The other two patients showed no more signs of the skin problem. The patient who had side effects from treatment stopped coming because the side effects were bad and happened often.

Diagnosis:
Porokeratosis (a skin condition that causes rough, scaly patches)

Instructions:
The patient should wear clothes that protect the skin from direct sunlight. The patient should keep taking isotretinoin 20mg pills. The patient should keep using halobetasol 0.05% cream as directed.

Hospital Course:
This 59-year-old woman came to the hospital with high fever, cough, and trouble breathing after getting flu shots. She was admitted to the hospital two weeks later because her symptoms suddenly got worse. This happened even though she had been taking antibiotics. Blood tests, scans, and a test that collects fluid from the lungs were done. These tests showed no signs of infection or cancer. More tests found swelling spread throughout both lungs. The patient also had weakness in muscles close to the body, like the upper arms and thighs. In January 2010, doctors determined she had a muscle disease called polymyositis along with lung swelling.

The patient got better with steroid medicine. Her overall health and muscle problems improved a lot during the first week of treatment. A detailed scan of the lungs showed the swelling had spread deeper into lung tissue. Because of this, doctors added another medicine called mycophenolate mofetil during the fifth week of steroid treatment. Right now, the muscle disease is still slightly active. The patient also has widespread body pain and feelings of sadness. The patient left the hospital after responding well to treatment and becoming stable.

Diagnosis:

Admitting Diagnosis: Twisted intestines (intestinal malrotation)

Principal Diagnosis at Discharge: Twisted intestines fixed with surgery to connect two parts of the small intestine

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 14-day-old baby girl, was admitted to our hospital because of green fluid coming up through her feeding tube. She was born 9 weeks early in poor health. She needed a breathing tube with a special breathing machine, medicines to support her heart, and medicine to help her lungs. Before birth, doctors found that her heart was on the right side instead of the left. Her stomach was also on the wrong side. These findings were confirmed after birth.

During the physical exam, the patient looked normal on the outside. Her belly exam showed nothing unusual. An X-ray of her belly showed normal air patterns matching her reversed organ positions. A special X-ray test using dye showed her intestines were twisted. The patient needed emergency surgery through a cut on the upper left side of her belly. During surgery, doctors found her stomach was on the right side. There were tissue bands connecting parts of her intestines. A blood vessel was crossing in front of part of her small intestine. Doctors cut the tissue bands causing problems. They decided to connect two parts of the small intestine together. They sewed the connection in a diamond shape in front of the misplaced blood vessel using dissolvable stitches.

After surgery, the patient recovered well without problems. Tube feeding started on the second day after surgery. Feeds were slowly increased to full amounts over 2 weeks. At clinic visits at 3 months and 1 year old, the patient was eating well. She was having regular bowel movements. She was not throwing up. She was gaining weight as expected.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was sent home on (date) in good health and drinking well by mouth. The parents were told to keep feeding the patient as they have been doing. They were also told to watch how well the patient handles feedings, has bowel movements, and gains weight at regular check-ups with the regular doctor. The parents were told to get medical help right away if they have any concerns.

Follow-up appointments:

The patient should see the regular children's doctor at their normal scheduled visits.

Signed,

(Physician's Name) MD

Hospital Course Summary:

Subjective:

The patient is a 65-year-old female with mouth cancer that came back. She came to our facility after the cancer returned in the area near her throat on the left side. The patient had radiation and chemotherapy to her neck area. She was then sent to our unit to join a new treatment study.

Objective:

During the initial tests, chest scans showed hazy spots in the lungs. These spots suggested a possible COVID-19 infection. Blood tests showed the patient had been exposed to the COVID-19 virus before. The patient had no symptoms. Two nose swab tests came back negative for active infection. The patient started a new treatment plan. She received an immune therapy drug through an IV every three weeks. She also took a cancer-blocking pill every day. The first scans showed the cancer stayed about the same size. The hazy spots in both lower parts of her lungs got bigger.

Assessment and Plan:

More tests showed no signs of cancer in the lungs. The lung tissue showed swelling, immune cell buildup, and damage to air sacs. These findings matched lung irritation caused by the immune therapy. The immune therapy drug likely made the hazy lung spots worse. The earlier COVID-19 infection may have made the lungs more likely to react to the immune therapy. The daily cancer pill probably did not cause the lung problem. The patient had a needle test of her lung tissue guided by a scanner. The test results confirmed lung irritation from the immune therapy. The lung problem was mild and the patient had no symptoms. The cancer was responding well to treatment. The patient started the immune therapy again. She was still receiving treatment when she left the hospital.

Plan:

The patient should follow these instructions after leaving the hospital. She must keep all appointments with her regular doctor and cancer doctor. These visits are important while she is on treatment. She will need regular scans to watch for any changes in the lung irritation. She will need continued scans to check her lungs. Tests to check how well her lungs work are important. She must tell her doctors right away if she has any breathing problems.

Prognosis:

The patient is expected to do well. She will keep receiving the study treatment for her returning mouth cancer.

The patient had a brain scan using a special dye. The scan showed signs of long-term high pressure inside the skull. These signs included bending of the eye nerves, widening of fluid spaces around the brain, flattening at the back of the eyes, and an empty space where a gland should be. Another test looking at blood vessels in the brain showed that a growth was pressing on a major vein on the right side of the head. Because this growth was causing high pressure in the brain veins, the doctors decided to remove it with surgery. The surgery was done through a cut behind the right ear. The growth was fully removed, and the vein pressure went down right away. Lab tests showed the growth was a type of bone tumor called an osteoblastoma.

POSTOPERATIVE COURSE:
After surgery, the patient developed an infection in the bone behind the right ear. This infection was treated successfully. The headaches went away quickly. The patient's vision slowly got better over the following weeks. At a 4-week eye checkup, vision was 7 out of 10 in the right eye and 4 out of 10 in the left eye. The swelling at the back of the eyes was completely gone. There was some lasting damage to the left eye nerve. A brain scan 4 months later showed the pressed vein was now normal size. The signs of high pressure in the skull had greatly improved.

DISCHARGE PLAN:
The patient was sent home and told to come back for a follow-up visit. The patient and family were told to contact their doctor if the headaches, neck pain, or vision problems come back.

MEDICATIONS:
None.

A hospital visit to check on the patient's condition will be scheduled within the next month.

The patient came to the hospital with a bad headache that was getting worse. She also had a stiff neck, fever, and sensitivity to light. She felt sick to her stomach, threw up, and had back pain. The patient had kidney stones in the past but was not taking any medicines at home. She had no allergies. No one in her family had high blood pressure, heart disease, or cancer. The patient had been on vacation in Massachusetts. She spent a lot of time outside and went swimming. She did not notice any insect bites.

During the physical exam, doctors found a rash with small blisters on one side of her body. The rash went from her mid-back area to under her left breast. Her neck was stiff. All other exam results were normal. The patient was awake and knew who she was, where she was, and what day it was.

A scan of her head showed no stroke, bleeding, or tumors. Tests on her spinal fluid found no germs. Blood tests also came back negative. Tests for Lyme disease, West Nile Virus, and herpes viruses all came back negative at first.

Doctors started treatment with two antibiotics given through an IV. They also gave her medicine to fight viruses and a steroid to reduce swelling. The spinal fluid was sent to the health department for more testing. Her white blood cell count was normal at 5.2 times 10 to the third cells per microliter. Other blood tests were also normal. Later tests showed the virus that causes chickenpox and shingles was in her spinal fluid. The patient was sent home with antiviral pills.

The patient felt better with less headache and fever. By day five in the hospital, doctors stopped the steroid medicine. After going home, the patient said she felt well. Her stiff neck and fever were gone.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient had an infection of the lining around her brain and spinal cord. This was caused by the chickenpox and shingles virus.

Discharge Medications:
The patient went home with antiviral pills called acyclovir.

Follow-up:
The patient should keep taking the antiviral pills. She should see her regular doctor for a follow-up visit.

Surgery to create an opening in the bladder and surgery to create a proper bottom opening and fix the bowel.

The baby went home in stable condition and is doing well at 19 months after birth.

The baby will be watched for any new problems as he grows. He will have regular visits with a children's doctor.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Date of admission: July 20, 2020
Date of discharge: September 21, 2020

Admission Diagnosis: COVID-19 infection, HIV infection

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 27-year-old male with HIV infection. He tested positive for COVID-19. He was admitted to our facility on July 20, 2020. He had trouble breathing and low oxygen levels for 10 days. He had general illness symptoms like fever and fatigue for about 12 days. He was taking his regular HIV medicines called nevirapine, lamivudine, and zidovudine. His vital signs showed fast breathing, fast heart rate, high blood pressure, and low oxygen. During the physical exam, the patient looked to be in good condition. His lungs sounded normal when listened to. Blood tests showed his liver was not working normally. He also had high levels of markers that show swelling and possible blood clots.

A scan of the chest showed hazy spots in the lungs. Another scan of the lung blood vessels showed no blood clots at that time. The patient was given several medicines. These included a blood thinner called enoxaparin, an antibiotic called ceftriaxone, and a steroid called dexamethasone. Even with a breathing mask, his breathing got worse. He needed a breathing tube placed in his throat, medicine to help him sleep, and care in the intensive care unit. After nine days, the patient left the intensive care unit. But he had to go back because of new trouble breathing, fast heart rate, and fever.

A heart ultrasound showed a blood clot in the upper right chamber of the heart. A new scan of the lung blood vessels showed blood clots in the left lung artery. The treatment was changed to address these problems. The blood thinner enoxaparin was increased to 80 mg two times daily. New medicines were added to fight infection. These included linezolid, anidulafungin, and sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim. The patient had unstable blood pressure and needed a medicine called noradrenaline to support it. A breathing tube with lying face down did not work. So a machine was used to pump and add oxygen to his blood outside his body. During treatment, the patient had some bleeding and got infections from three different germs.

After 30 days of treatment, the patient got better and left the hospital on September 21, 2020. When he left, he was given these medicines to take: fluconazole for fungal infection, sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim for infection prevention, rivaroxaban to prevent blood clots, omeprazole for stomach protection, and pain medicines.

Follow-up:

The patient kept seeing doctors at the outpatient clinic. He also did physical therapy exercises at home.

Disclaimer:

This discharge summary is based on the patient's medical record. It is provided only for information purposes. It is not meant to give medical diagnosis, treatment, or medical advice.

The patient came to our clinic with weakness in the left arm and leg that had lasted for 7 months. During the exam, the doctors found the left arm and leg could not move well. Treatment:

There is no medicine that has been shown to work for CCM. This is especially true when there are many small problem areas. For now, the patient and family members will be treated for their symptoms. This includes keeping blood pressure under control and treating headaches.

Follow-up:

The patient should see the doctor and a genetic counselor on a regular basis. The patient should let them know if anything changes or if new symptoms appear.

Discharge Condition:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 57-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Loss of smell and blockage in both sides of the nose

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with a 2-year history of blockage in both sides of the nose, worse on the right side, and loss of smell. He also reported moderate headache. An ear, nose, and throat exam showed a growth starting from the top of the nasal cavity on both sides, covering the area where smell is sensed. A camera exam of the nose showed the surface of the growth was uneven. The patient had a CT scan of the nose and surrounding air pockets. The scan showed a soft tissue growth in the smell-sensing area and swollen tissue shaped like small growths in the cheek air pockets on both sides. The scan also showed major swelling shaped like small growths in the air pockets between the eyes, behind the nose, and in the nasal cavities. The patient had no history of nosebleeds, runny nose, repeated sinus infections, or any brain or nerve problems.

Diagnosis:
Based on the CT scan of the nose and surrounding air pockets, the patient was found to have a soft tissue growth in both smell-sensing areas that reached up to the base of the skull. This suggested a type of tumor that starts in the smell-sensing nerve cells. The case was discussed in a team meeting with different specialists. The team agreed to remove the entire growth for testing rather than just taking a small sample. This would be done while the patient was fully asleep. The patient then had surgery using a camera through the nose to remove the growth from the thin bone at the top of the nasal cavity on both sides.

Treatment:
Surgery using a camera through the nose was done to remove both the smell-area growth and tissue from all four sets of air pockets. Small nose growths were also removed, and the wall between the nostrils was straightened. Recovery after surgery went smoothly with no problems. Lab testing of the growths from both sides showed nose and sinus lining tissue with fluid buildup under the surface, long-term swelling cells, and thickening of the base layer. These findings are usually seen in cases of nose and sinus small growths. However, deep folding of the surface tissue with false gland-like shapes is not a usual feature of nose and sinus small growths. A specialist in head and neck tissue testing gave a final diagnosis of nose and sinus small growths with a condition where gland tissue grows more than normal.

Follow-up:
The patient was seen in the clinic with regular camera exams of the nose. His nose blockage got better over time. However, he did not get his sense of smell back. The patient has been in our care for more than two years. His breathing through the nose is good. There is no return of sinus infections or small nose growths. The patient still has no sense of smell. Overall, he is happy with his current health regarding his nose problems and our treatment.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition is now stable, and he is being sent home.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of admission: [REDACTED]
Date of discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Bulge in a major blood vessel at the base of the brain
Discharge Diagnosis: Bulge in a major blood vessel at the base of the brain treated with a small tube to redirect blood flow

Hospital Course:
A 60-year-old male came to the hospital because of headaches. A special scan of his brain showed a bulge in a major blood vessel at the base of the brain. The bulge measured about 20 mm by 10 mm. Regular surgery could not fix this problem. The patient had other health issues including heart disease, an irregular heartbeat, a metal heart valve, a past stroke caused by blocked blood flow, high blood pressure, and a past blood clot in a leg vein.

The patient had a bypass surgery to create a new path to reach the bulge. The doctor made a cut in the right side of the neck to reach a main neck blood vessel. A vein was taken from the left thigh. This vein was connected to the neck blood vessel and to a blood vessel near the spine. A scan the next day showed blood was flowing well through the new path.

After surgery, the patient had low blood pressure. This was likely because the brain was adjusting blood flow after the bypass. The patient also got an infection from a medical tube. This delayed the second part of the treatment. Six weeks after the bypass, the doctor did another procedure. A thin tube was put into a blood vessel in the groin. The doctor guided the tube through the blood vessels to reach the bulge in the brain. A small mesh tube was placed to redirect blood flow away from the bulge. There were no major problems. The patient recovered well.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care physician. The patient should keep taking any prescribed medications. The patient should watch for signs of fever, swelling, or redness where the surgery was done. The patient should not do hard exercise or lift heavy things for at least 4 to 6 weeks.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to see their primary care physician within 2 to 4 weeks for a regular check-up. The patient should also make an appointment with their surgeon. This visit will check how the patient is healing and make sure they get the right care.

Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient came to our clinic for tests to check a growth that looked like it might be in the uterus. During the first exam, the uterus was larger than normal. A solid mass was found, but it was hard to tell where the growth ended and the uterus began. An MRI scan showed a tumor in the right side of the lower belly. The patient had surgery using a small camera to remove the right ovary and tube. During surgery, doctors found a 4-inch mass on the right ovary. The tumor had not spread or burst open. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed the tumor was a rare type of ovarian cancer called malignant ovarian fibrothecoma.

The patient then had more surgery to fully remove the cancer. Doctors removed the uterus, left ovary and tube, and a fatty tissue layer in the belly. Because all affected tissue was removed, the tumor is not expected to come back. In the two years since surgery, the tumor has not returned. The patient continues to have regular checkups.

Before leaving, the patient received information about her condition. She learned why follow-up care is important. A visit with her regular doctor has been set up. This doctor will continue to watch over her health.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Patient Age: 23 months old

Gender: Male

Reason for Hospital Stay: Suspected brain and spinal cord infection

Final Diagnosis: Rasmussen Encephalitis, a rare brain disease that causes swelling

Hospital Stay:

The patient came to the hospital with fever, extreme tiredness, sleepiness, and confusion. The doctor checked the nervous system and found a stiff neck. The patient could not sit up alone because of poor muscle control and weak muscles. Blood tests showed high white blood cell counts and high platelet counts. Other blood tests for infection and body salts were normal. A brain scan was normal. A spinal tap showed too many white blood cells, mostly one type called monocytes.

The patient received two medicines called acyclovir and ceftriaxone. The patient did not get better and got worse instead. Doctors did another spinal tap that showed normal white blood cell counts. A detailed brain scan called an MRI showed swelling in part of the brain stem. This matched a condition called Rasmussen Encephalitis. Doctors then gave strong steroid medicine through an IV. After that, the patient took steroid pills by mouth.

Tests for a disease where the body attacks itself came back negative. Over time, the patient slowly got better until fully recovered. The patient went home with steroid pills in smaller doses over four weeks. Over one year of checkups, the patient had no return of symptoms. Follow-up brain scans showed the swelling went away completely.

Medicines to Take at Home:

Steroid pills in slowly decreasing doses for four weeks

Condition at Discharge:

The patient went home in good health with no problems.

Follow-up Appointments:

Brain and nerve doctor visit in one week
Brain scan in six months

The patient came to our department for special care. The patient had a painless lump on the jaw that grew slowly over 3 years. The patient also lost some teeth during this time. The doctor found a large, sore lump that made the lower lip stick out. Inside the mouth, there was a hard lump about 2 inches wide. This lump pushed the teeth out of place so they did not line up right. Pictures of the jaw showed a large growth that was destroying bone and had a hollow space inside. The head doctor of our department did the surgery. The doctor removed a hollow growth that had no fluid inside. The outer wall of the jawbone had broken through, but the bone did not break during surgery. The patient took medicine to fight infection and control pain every day for 8 days. The patient healed well after surgery.

Recommendations:
The patient was told to get dental work to fix the teeth and mouth. The patient came back for check-up visits at 3, 6, and 12 months. There were no signs the growth came back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: A type of blood cancer called chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) at a moderate stage.

Hospital Course:

The patient is an 80-year-old man with a history of high blood pressure. The patient was admitted to [Redacted] Hospital on [Redacted] because of increasing belly swelling. The patient was diagnosed with a blood cancer called chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Blood tests showed too many white blood cells, especially a type called lymphocytes. The patient had been receiving treatment for this condition for 15 years.

A full body scan showed many small swollen lymph nodes in the neck, chest, and belly area. The scan also showed an enlarged spleen with a swollen node nearby. The patient had a bone marrow test done by taking a small sample from the bone. The test showed that cancer cells made up about 72.5% of the bone marrow sample. Additional testing found changes in the genes of the cancer cells. These findings confirmed the diagnosis of CLL at a moderate stage.

One year after the diagnosis, the patient started taking a cancer medicine called chlorambucil twice daily. This was because the number of abnormal white blood cells kept rising. After 11 months of treatment, the blood cell counts went back to normal. However, 18 months after starting chlorambucil, the patient developed painless belly swelling. The patient did not have fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

Blood tests showed low red blood cell counts and low platelet counts. Kidney function and protein levels in the blood were normal. Heart tests showed the heart was working well. An ultrasound of the belly ruled out liver scarring. Tests for liver infections (hepatitis B and C) were negative. Fluid that built up in the belly contained mostly lymphocytes. A belly scan showed enlarged lymph nodes in the belly area that had gotten worse since the first scan.

Lab tests on the fluid from the belly showed that 80% of the cells were lymphocytes. Most of these were not normal T cells or B cells. Special testing found abnormal cancer cells in the belly fluid. The patient had a surgery using a small camera to look inside the belly. This was done to rule out infection, a new cancer, or the cancer becoming more aggressive. The surgery found a lot of fluid and many small white lymph nodes on the belly lining. A small tissue sample from a lymph node showed abnormal cell growth. Special staining tests confirmed that the CLL had spread to the belly lining.

The patient was treated with a steroid medicine called prednisolone and the cancer medicine chlorambucil. The belly fluid went away quickly and was gone after one month. The patient was sent home with instructions to see their regular doctor and cancer doctor. These doctors will continue to manage the CLL that has spread to the belly lining.

Disposition: Discharged
Follow-up: The patient will see their regular doctor and cancer doctor as an outpatient.

Hospital Course Summary:

Hospital Day 1:
A 31-year-old African-American female came to the emergency room with sudden, severe headaches. These headaches strongly suggested bleeding around the brain. A brain and nerve exam showed no problems.

Hospital Day 2:
A brain scan showed bleeding around the brain, mostly on the left side. There was also a mild buildup of fluid in the brain. Another scan showed a larger than normal blood vessel on the left side of the brain. A detailed imaging test of the blood vessels showed an oddly shaped blood vessel in that area. No treatment was done at that time.

Hospital Day 14:
The patient stayed stable in the brain surgery intensive care unit. The care team did regular brain and nerve exams and daily tests to check blood flow in the brain. These tests showed only moderate narrowing of the blood vessels. The patient did not need treatment for the mild fluid buildup seen on the scans. On Day 14, the patient had another detailed blood vessel imaging test. It showed ongoing blood vessel narrowing in some arteries at the back of the brain. The test also showed a weakened, bulging section of a blood vessel on the left side of the brain. No treatment was done at that time.

Hospital Day 21:
The patient had a successful procedure done through the blood vessels. Doctors placed a small mesh tube to cover the weakened, bulging section of the blood vessel. This section was 3 millimeters wide and 18 millimeters long. The goal was to keep blood flowing normally while redirecting blood away from the weak area. This would help the weak area shrink and eventually close off.

Hospital Day 90:
At the 3-month follow-up visit, the patient was stable with no brain or nerve problems and no complaints. A scan showed the blood vessel was open above and below the mesh tube. There were no signs of bulging or a weak spot in the blood vessel.

Hospital Day 300:
At the 10-month follow-up visit, a detailed blood vessel imaging test showed the weak area had healed. The blood vessel stayed open. There was mild bending of the blood vessel caused by the mesh tube. The patient was stable with no brain or nerve problems and no complaints.

Final Diagnosis:
Bleeding around the brain caused by a weakened, bulging section of a blood vessel on the left side of the brain.

Interventions and Procedures:
Placement of a small mesh tube to cover the weakened, bulging section of the blood vessel.

Condition at Discharge:
Stable with no brain or nerve problems.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient chose not to have a follow-up imaging test done through a tube in the blood vessels.

Other Instructions:
None specified.

Patient Name: Not specified in case report
Gender: Male
Age: 34
Medical Record Number: Not specified in case report
Admission Date: Not specified in case report
Discharge Date: Not specified in case report
Length of Stay: Not specified in case report

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with on-and-off pain in the upper right belly and yellowing of the skin for 1 month. A physical exam showed dull and darkish skin color, yellow skin, a swollen belly, and signs of fluid in the belly. A blood protein called IgG4 was high in the patient, his younger sister, and his daughter.

Blood tests showed no problems with hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or other liver-related antibodies. There were no issues with blood or urine digestive enzymes or cancer markers. A special scan of the liver showed scarring of the liver and slight widening of some bile tubes inside the liver.

A small piece of liver tissue was taken for testing. It showed scarring around the bile tubes, a buildup of certain white blood cells, and bile buildup in liver cells near the portal area. Special staining showed only a few scattered IgG-positive cells. IgG4 staining showed very few IgG4-positive cells (1 to 3 cells per viewing field).

At first, doctors thought the patient had an IgG4-related bile duct disease. They started steroid pills at 40 mg per day, but the yellow skin did not get better. The patient got worse and had serious problems after steroid treatment. A tube with a camera was used to look at the bile ducts and showed uneven narrowing of the bile tubes inside the liver. A drainage tube was placed through the nose into the bile duct. A camera exam of the large intestine showed long-term inflammation. Doctors strongly suspected a disease called primary sclerosing cholangitis based on no response to steroids and the camera test findings.

The patient had a liver transplant when his body functions were stable. Testing of the removed liver during surgery showed scarring, shrunken bile duct cells, and a ring-like scarring pattern in the portal area. Special staining showed only a few scattered IgG-positive cells. IgG4 staining showed very few IgG4-positive cells (1 to 3 cells per viewing field). These findings matched primary sclerosing cholangitis. After the liver transplant, the patient's quality of life got much better.

One year after the liver transplant, the IgG4 blood protein levels in the patient, his younger sister, and his daughter were above normal. Genetic testing showed that both the patient and his younger sister had the same gene type. His daughter had a related gene type. Three years after the liver transplant, liver blood tests showed that ALT and AST levels were normal. A belly ultrasound showed no clear problems.

Summary:
The 34-year-old male patient with on-and-off pain in the upper right belly and yellow skin for 1 month was found to have liver scarring and slight widening of some bile tubes inside the liver. Doctors first thought he had an IgG4-related bile duct disease and started steroid pills, but the yellow skin did not improve. The patient was diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis based on no response to steroids and camera test findings. He had a liver transplant when his body functions were stable. One year after the liver transplant, IgG4 blood protein levels were above normal in the patient, his younger sister, and his daughter. Genetic testing showed shared gene types in the family. Three years after the liver transplant, liver blood tests showed ALT and AST were normal. A belly ultrasound showed no clear problems. The patient's quality of life got much better after the liver transplant.

Medical History:
The patient is a 51-year-old male who came to the emergency room with sudden belly pain and feeling sick to his stomach. He was told he had COVID-19 one week before and was staying home to recover.

Hospital Course:
During his stay, doctors found a blood clot in a main blood vessel that supplies the gut. This clot was blocking blood flow to parts of his intestine. The patient needed emergency surgery to open his belly and remove the blood clot. About 45 cm of his small intestine had died from lack of blood and had to be removed. He had two more surgeries to check his belly. During these, doctors removed another 10 cm of dead small intestine. They also connected the remaining small intestine to the large intestine. After a third surgery to close his belly, the patient was taken off the breathing machine. He spent six days in the intensive care unit before moving to a step-down unit. He was later moved to a regular hospital room. He stayed in the hospital for almost forty days before going home. When he left, he had fully recovered. He was told to come back for check-up visits.

Final Diagnosis:
Blood clot in a main blood vessel supplying the gut, which caused parts of the intestine to lose blood flow.

Treatment:
Emergency surgery to open the belly and remove the blood clot, removal of dead small intestine, follow-up surgeries to check the belly, connection of small intestine to large intestine, and plenty of fluids through an IV. Blood-thinning medicine was given through an IV and adjusted based on hospital guidelines.

Follow-up:
The patient was told to come back for check-up visits.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Age: 20-year-old male
Reason for Admission: Slow-starting pain in the upper right belly area

Hospital Course:
The patient had pain in the upper right belly area that started slowly over one month. The pain came with feeling sick to the stomach, throwing up, not feeling hungry, yellow color in the whites of the eyes, itching, pale bowel movements, and dark urine. The patient had no past health problems or surgeries. Tests at another hospital found a mass near the pancreas pressing on the main bile tube. Three weeks before coming to us, doctors did a procedure to open the bile tube and placed a small plastic tube to keep it open. Blood tests showed high levels of a yellow substance called bilirubin and high liver test numbers. An ultrasound of the belly showed a dark-colored mass near the pancreas measuring about 4.8 by 3.2 centimeters with little blood flow. An MRI scan of the belly showed a fluid-filled mass behind the head of the pancreas with no swollen lymph nodes in the belly. A cell test showed damaged lymph node tissue and tested positive for tuberculosis germs. The patient started taking four medicines to treat tuberculosis: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. At follow-up visits, the patient gained 4 kilograms of weight and liver test numbers returned to normal after one month of treatment. The patient finished 9 months of tuberculosis treatment with no problems. The plastic tube was then taken out, and the bilirubin level stayed normal at later follow-up visits.

Diagnosis:
Damaged lymph node tissue caused by tuberculosis

Recommendations:
The patient should have regular follow-up visits to make sure of full recovery.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 65-year-old African American man with a history of diabetes and gout. He came to the hospital with right third toe pain, on and off fever, and chills. The doctors checked his toe and found it was purple and black in color. The toe was swollen and soft but did not hurt when touched. When pressed, the tool went all the way to the bone. An X-ray showed that the tip of the small toe bone was missing. There was also damage to the soft tissue around it. Lab tests found two types of bacteria called Escherichia coli and coagulase-negative staphylococci. After five days, no more bacteria grew in the tests. The patient had several surgeries to clean out the infected tissue. This was needed because of a bone infection. The doctors had to remove part of the foot bone connected to the third toe. Later, the patient started having new pain in his right knee. Tests on the knee fluid showed it was cloudy and milky. The fluid had signs of gout, including special crystals. The doctors said he had gout in his knee. Blood tests showed his white blood cell count was slowly going up. Most of these cells were a type called monocytes. About 22 out of every 100 cells seen were very young blood cells called blasts. The blood sample also showed cells with an unusual shape. This raised concerns about a problem with how blood cells are made. More blood tests confirmed the patient has a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia or AML. The test found a specific change in the cells called Inv(16). This change means the cancer may respond well to treatment. Once the patient was stable, he was moved to a cancer center. There he will receive treatment for his blood cancer.

Discharge Summary

Patient Information:
Name: Not provided
Sex: Female
Age: 76 years

Hospital Course:
The patient had heart valve replacement surgeries in 1989 and 2009. These surgeries replaced damaged valves that control blood flow in the heart.
In 2010, the patient had dark, bloody stools and went into shock from blood loss. This was caused by abnormal blood vessels in the lower part of the large intestine. The patient needed blood transfusions to become stable. Doctors used a camera tool to find and seal the bleeding spots.
Between 2010 and 2016, the patient had several bleeding episodes in the stomach and intestines. These were caused by abnormal blood vessels, sores, and growths in different areas. Doctors used camera tools to clip and seal the bleeding spots.
In 2016, the patient had low blood levels due to a bleeding growth in the stomach. This was linked to a bacterial infection called H. pylori. Doctors removed the growth and treated the infection. However, the low blood levels returned in 2017.
In 2017, a tiny camera pill found abnormal blood vessels in the small intestine. Doctors treated these using a special heat tool. The patient needed 360 units of blood between 2017 and 2020 due to ongoing low blood levels.
In October 2020, the patient vomited blood due to many abnormal blood vessels in the stomach. Doctors stopped the bleeding twice using a heat tool.
The patient died in November 2020 from sudden worsening of long-term heart failure. This was 10 years after the first bleeding episode.

Medical History:
Heart valve replacement surgeries in 1989
Heart valve replacement surgery in 2009
Bleeding episodes in the stomach and intestines from abnormal blood vessels, sores, and growths between 2010 and 2016
Low blood levels from a bleeding stomach growth caused by H. pylori infection in 2016
Abnormal blood vessels in the small intestine found and treated in 2017
Many abnormal blood vessels in the stomach treated in October 2020

Diagnostic Assessment:
Blood tests showed a hemoglobin level of 11.0 g/dL after the 2010 episode. Hemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.
The speed of blood flow through the heart valve was 3.96 m/s in 2008. It dropped to 3.04 m/s after surgery in 2009.
Blood flow speed rose to 3.95 m/s in 2010 when bleeding started. It increased to 4.74 m/s in 2012.
A protein that helps blood clot dropped from 113% in 2017 to 100% in 2019.
Testing of this clotting protein showed normal results in 2020.
A protein that helps blood vessels grow was 865 pg/mL. The normal range is 62 to 704 pg/mL.

Summary and Follow-up:
The patient had several bleeding episodes in the stomach and intestines between 2010 and 2016. These were caused by abnormal blood vessels and treated with camera tools.
Low blood levels returned in 2016 due to a bleeding stomach growth caused by H. pylori infection. Later, abnormal blood vessels in the small intestine were found and treated with a heat tool.
Many abnormal blood vessels in the stomach caused the patient to vomit blood in October 2020. Doctors treated these with a heat tool.
Sadly, the patient died in November 2020 from sudden worsening of long-term heart failure.
No further follow-up is required.

They removed it. Tests showed it was a cluster of abnormal blood vessels that had bled several times.

In 2008, brain scans showed a new growth in the same spot as the first one from 2002. Doctors also found another growth in a different part of the brain. In 2009, doctors removed the growth on the left side of the brain. Tests showed this growth had two types of tissue mixed together. One part was the same type as before, and one part was abnormal blood vessels.

Brain scans after surgery showed no growth was left behind. The other growth in the brain seemed to be getting smaller on its own. Doctors did not suggest any extra treatment. Both types of growths were not cancer, and one was shrinking by itself. The patient left the hospital in good health.

The patient left the hospital in good health. Brain scans showed no signs of the growth coming back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Date of Admission: August 4, 2015
Sex: Male
Date of Discharge: N/A
Age: 6 years old
Length of Stay: N/A

History and Findings:
The patient is a 6-year-old boy who came in because he was losing vision in both eyes quickly over 38 days. The patient had mild trouble seeing at night starting one year before coming to the hospital. The patient's eyesight kept getting worse over time. When the patient arrived at the eye center, the pressure inside his eyes was normal. Doctors found many small bumps on the colored part of both eyes. The nerves at the back of both eyes looked pale, and the blood vessels in the eyes were thin. The middle outer areas of the back of both eyes looked spotted, but there were no dark bone-shaped spots. Other body exams showed no problems.

Diagnostic Tests and Results:
A special dye test of the eyes showed bright and dark spotted areas at the back of the eyes. A scan of the eye layers showed thinning and damage in the outer layer of the back of the eye, but the center vision area was still intact. Tests that measure how the eyes respond to light showed no activity in both eyes. No brain response to light flashes was found either. A brain scan showed several spots where the protective covering of nerves was damaged in the right front and side parts of the brain. Both eye nerves were also larger than normal.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient was found to have a condition that damages the back of the eye and causes vision loss, along with swelling of the eye nerves. The patient was given a medicine to reduce swelling for 14 days, then the dose was slowly lowered. After treatment, the patient's vision with glasses slowly got better. The patient also had a gene test that found a change in a gene called OFD1, which was passed down from family members.

Main Problem: Belly pain that came and went, along with bloating

What Happened Before Coming to the Hospital:
A 57-year-old man who had a heart procedure in the past came in with belly pain and bloating that came and went. The patient said there was no recent injury. Blood tests showed a higher than normal level of a clotting protein. A CT scan of the belly found several dense lumps blocking part of the lower bowel. A camera test of the bowel showed a growth under the bowel lining with normal tissue on top and some bleeding. The growth was almost fully blocking the bowel passage. The patient was found to have a blood clot inside the wall of the lower bowel.

Because of the blood clotting problem, blood-thinning medicines were stopped. Treatment focused on rest for the bowel. The patient received nutrition through an IV line and fluids through a vein. The patient did not need any blood given. A follow-up CT scan done 1 month later showed the lumps in the bowel were completely gone. The patient was sent home on cilostazol and clopidogrel instead of aspirin. No new bleeding happened during the 1-year check-up period.

The patient was in stable condition when leaving the hospital.

The patient should see a stomach and bowel doctor as an outpatient.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]
Patient Name: [Patient's name]
Medical Record Number: [Patient's medical record number]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 43-year-old man with no previous health problems. He came to the hospital with a headache, a drooping left eyelid, and double vision. He had no other brain or nerve problems. Eye doctors and brain doctors examined him. A scan of the head and blood vessels was done to check for a bulge in a brain artery. No bulge was found. More detailed scans of the head and eye area were also normal.

While in the hospital, the patient developed stomach pain that got worse after eating. A sound wave test of the belly showed the bowel wall might be thick. A detailed scan of the belly showed thickening and uneven edges of the small intestine wall. It also showed swollen glands in both groin areas. A scan of the chest was done to check for swollen glands there. It showed a large blockage in the right upper heart chamber. This blockage extended into the large vein leading to the heart. This finding suggested a type of blood cancer.

More tests were done, including a heart sound wave test and a detailed heart scan. These showed a growth inside the heart that matched blood cancer. A sample was taken from a swollen gland. The sample showed signs of a fast-growing blood cancer.

The patient was then moved to a cancer hospital for treatment. Treatment began with a drug plan called CHOP. This included four medicines: cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone. Medicine was also given through a needle in the spine. At first, the patient got better. Later, the patient got worse and passed away.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was found to have Burkitt lymphoma. This is a fast-growing blood cancer. It was found using the chest scan and the gland sample.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was sent to a cancer comfort care center for end-of-life care. The family was told to keep giving the patient's medicines as directed. They were told to stay in contact with the comfort care team. The family was also told to call emergency services if any urgent health problems came up.
